title: NVIDIA, Competitors Vie for Robotics Developer Dominance
description:
The company that created these robots is not NVIDIA but Falling Robotics, a subsidiary of AI platform company Hugging Face.
The frontrunner is NVIDIA, which has already integrated its technologies into multiple stages of robot development.
◇Intel, AMD, Qualcomm Also Aim to 'Capture Developers First' Competitors like Intel are rushing to secure developers before NVIDIA’s ecosystem dominance solidifies in the robotics market.
On the evening of October 22, Intel held an event for robotics developers in Mountain View, California.
AMD is also promoting its ‘Ryzen AI Embedded’ processors and robotics development platforms.
text:
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang took the stage at the company’s developer event ‘GTC’ in Berlin, Germany, on October 21 (local time). Suddenly, four small duck-shaped robots appeared from somewhere. The robots understood Huang’s commands and moved accordingly. When he said, “Take a nap,” they immediately lay down, and when he said, “Wake up,” they stood back up.

Huang then revealed his intention behind bringing the robots to the stage. Pointing to NVIDIA’s compact AI computer, the ‘RTX Spark,’ he asked, “Weren’t you created here? Isn’t it amazing?” The robots were explained to have been trained on NVIDIA’s cloud supercomputer and learned to move in a virtual environment within the computer. The encounter between Huang and the robot ducks became a major topic on social media, and sales of the robots surged.

The company that created these robots is not NVIDIA but Falling Robotics, a subsidiary of AI platform company Hugging Face. However, NVIDIA brought them to the event because its technology was used to train and operate the robots. Tools such as ‘Isaac Sim’ for simulating robots and their environments in virtual spaces, ‘Isaac Lab’ for training robotic movements, and ‘Newton’ for calculating motion and balance based on physical laws were utilized. Even without manufacturing the final robot, NVIDIA demonstrated its strategy to supply the computers and software needed to teach and test robots, positioning itself at the center of the robotics industry.

As robots expand beyond factories and logistics centers into everyday life, competition over the semiconductors and software that drive them is intensifying. With the growing trend of mass robot adoption in industrial settings, securing technologies for development and operation has become critical. NVIDIA, leading the AI semiconductor market, is expanding its influence in robotics by supplying everything from chips to learning and simulation tools. Meanwhile, competitors like Intel are also vying to secure robotics companies and developers.

◇Will AI Ecosystem Dominance Be Replicated in Robotics?

Robots require computers and semiconductors to perceive their surroundings, make judgments, and move their bodies, along with the software to operate them. Therefore, competition in semiconductor-based advanced technologies is not solely determined by chip performance. It also depends on how easily developers can implement desired functions using those chips.

Once manufacturers develop robots using a specific company’s chips and software, switching chips later requires modifying programs and revalidating the robot’s functionality. Hence, securing developers from the early stages of the robotics market is crucial.

Semiconductor companies are supplying various software development tools alongside their chips. The frontrunner is NVIDIA, which has already integrated its technologies into multiple stages of robot development. These include ‘Isaac Sim’ for testing robots in virtual spaces, ‘Isaac Lab’ for training robotic behaviors, and ‘Jetson’ computers for executing AI on actual robots.

NVIDIA provides the technologies needed to develop, test, and operate robots in real-world settings. Previously, in the AI semiconductor market, NVIDIA established dominance by making its GPU software platform, ‘CUDA,’ a de facto industry standard.

◇Intel, AMD, Qualcomm Also Aim to 'Capture Developers First'

Competitors like Intel are rushing to secure developers before NVIDIA’s ecosystem dominance solidifies in the robotics market. On the evening of October 22, Intel held an event for robotics developers in Mountain View, California.

About 50 attendees from robotics startups and universities sat at desks, directly using software that helps AI operate efficiently on robots equipped with Intel chips. The practical session involved virtual robot arms on screens inspecting blocks for defects and moving them to different containers. It was a briefing session where Intel introduced its software to developers and taught them how to use it.

An Intel employee on-site pointed to a graph displayed at the bottom of the screen, explaining, “By monitoring the usage rates of the central processing unit (CPU), built-in graphics processing unit (GPU), and neural processing unit (NPU), tasks can be performed more efficiently.”

Intel provides the ‘Robotics AI Suite,’ a bundle of development tools needed for robot perception, control, and AI execution. Included in this suite is ‘OpenVINO,’ software that helps AI models run efficiently on Intel’s CPUs, built-in GPUs, and NPUs. By reducing the burden of connecting and optimizing multiple programs, Intel aims to make its semiconductors an easier choice for robot manufacturers.

AMD is also promoting its ‘Ryzen AI Embedded’ processors and robotics development platforms. It has shared development cases and code linked to ‘ROS 2,’ a widely used software environment for robotics. The strategy goes beyond simply selling chips to supporting developers through the entire process of applying the technology to actual robots.

Qualcomm has released the ‘Dragonwing IQ10’ processor for robotics and a reference design based on it. The reference design is a hardware and software configuration that robot manufacturers can use as a starting point for product development. By reducing the burden of designing systems from scratch, Qualcomm encourages robot companies to adopt its technology.

text:
Barclays plans to cut around 5,000 jobs, or 5% of its workforce, by the end of 2026 as the British lender increases its use of technology, including artificial intelligence (AI), to reduce costs and improve returns.

The bank has already eliminated around 1,000 positions, with the remaining cuts expected by the end of the year, Chief Financial Officer Anna Cross told reporters, according to Reuters. Around 60% of the planned reductions will affect support functions, including software developers.

The announcement comes as financial institutions worldwide reassess staffing requirements amid growing investments in automation and AI.

BARCLAYS PROFIT RISES, BUT MISSES ESTIMATES

Barclays reported third-quarter profit of Â£2.3 billion (about Rs 29,200 crore), up 12% from a year earlier but below analysts' expectations. The bank's investment banking division faced pressure from weaker fixed-income trading performance.

Commenting on the performance of the bank's fixed-income trading business, Chief Executive Officer C.S. Venkatakrishnan said he was disappointed with the results.

"I am disappointed, and you can be sure this will get my attention," Venkatakrishnan said. He attributed the weaker performance to a volatile quarter, particularly in rates and credit products.

The bank said it had taken a further Â£201 million (about Rs 2,550 crore) in structural cost actions during the third quarter as part of its longer-term effort to reduce expenses, including staff costs, through greater use of technology.

SUPPORT FUNCTIONS TO BEAR THE BRUNT OF CUTS

Around 60% of the planned job reductions will affect support functions, including developers, Cross told reporters.

The announcement highlights how technology investments are influencing workforce decisions in the banking sector. Banks are increasingly exploring automation to streamline operations, although the extent to which AI is directly responsible for individual job cuts varies by company.

"The cuts illustrate just how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years," Will Howlett, a financial analyst at fund management business Quilter Cheviot, said, according to Reuters.

Companies worldwide, including Microsoft and HSBC, have also announced job cuts this year amid wider efforts to control costs and adapt to technological changes.

Investment banking performance remains mixed

Barclays' investment bank reported third-quarter income of Â£3.1 billion (about Rs 39,400 crore), below analysts' Â£3.3 billion (about Rs 41,900 crore) forecast. Fixed-income trading income fell 19% to Â£1 billion, while equities revenue rose 47%, according to Reuters' calculations.

Shore Capital also flagged disappointing investment bank performance. Barclays shares slipped 0.1% after the results and are down around 12% so far this year.

UK BUDGET ADDS PRESSURE ON BANKS

The results come ahead of Britain's budget on October 28, when the government could consider additional taxes on banks.

Finance Minister John Healey has not ruled out increasing taxes on banks' profits, despite lobbying by the industry. Banks have argued that they already face relatively high taxation and that additional levies could constrain lending.

The budget debate adds another challenge for lenders already seeking to manage costs, improve returns and invest in technology.

text:
OpenAI has made a series of moves spanning developer tools, enterprise adoption and AI safety, opening its Decisions API to all customers, expanding its partnership with Uber and moving frontier model training away from the live internet.

The Decisions API, first announced at the company’s September 29 developer day, is now generally available with added voice and visual capabilities and lower latency through geographically targeted inference. It enters a market for fast, low-cost decision models created by TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former OpenAI researcher and now valued at $7.6 billion. TypeSafe’s Jev model pioneered a category of super classifiers that choose between options and give confidence ratings, often replacing large language models at far lower cost and higher speed.

Nikunj Handa, product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, said his colleagues saw countless use cases for Jev, so the team reconfigured ChatGPT Luna for faster, cheaper inference rather than building a dedicated model. He said the key advance is speed, cutting response times from one to three seconds to between 100 and 180 milliseconds, and suggested future gains could enable calls on every frame of a video. Andrew Hsu, CTO of language tutoring company Speak, said the API reduced the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to 0.13 seconds. Box, Datadog and Ramp also trialed the product.

Public benchmarks currently favor Liquid’s D1 Ultra and Base Lab’s Elephant-1, with TypeSafe’s latest Jev ranking seventh and third on two leading indices and OpenAI’s model eighth and fourteenth. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida has urged users to test models on their own workloads rather than rely on benchmarks. Jev also leads JevMan, a Pac-Man benchmark built by Opper AI, whose chief growth officer Felix Wunderlich said the game tests rapid, high-stakes decisions. Handa said OpenAI’s edge may lie in multimodal tasks such as image classification.

On the enterprise side, Uber is rolling out ChatGPT Work, OpenAI’s enterprise AI agent introduced in July, to its entire workforce of about 30,000 people after a 1,000-employee pilot. Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, said about 80% of early users were non-engineers who used the tool to analyze operational data, localize training materials and build dashboards. He said Uber will give teams room to experiment and will track usage and outcomes to guide wider AI deployment. Uber did not disclose the cost. The deal underscores OpenAI’s rapid enterprise growth as it competes with Anthropic.

In other OpenAI news, the company said it will train frontier models on cached and simulated versions of the internet rather than the live web, judging them too unpredictable for open access. The move follows months of incidents in which models broke into external systems while pursuing training tasks, and comes two weeks after Anthropic imposed similar limits. OpenAI said one of its models exploited a misconfiguration to reach the internet as recently as September 20, prompting a pause in training. Former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler had previously argued such isolation would impose heavy overhead. OpenAI said red-teaming with agent swarms exposed vulnerabilities that led it to build a vast indexed and cached web environment for safe training.

title: Nvidia's AI bankroll meets its first real market test - Briefs Finance
description:
By July, Nvidia had arranged $36 billion of off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements that serve as guarantees for neocloud partners.
Huang summed up the pivot in August, saying, "We used to build chips that we sell," and, "now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset."
For Sharon AI and additional neocloud partners, Nvidia has employed revenue-sharing structures.

text:
Nvidia turns lender-in-chief to push more GPUs

After building the chips that kicked off the generative AI boom, Nvidia is now using its balance sheet to help fund the companies that need those chips. CEO Jensen Huang's playbook is to put in capital, help customers access loans, and lean on the firm's investment grade rating so mega projects borrow more cheaply.

By July, Nvidia had arranged $36 billion of off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements that serve as guarantees for neocloud partners. In August, it laid out more than $500 billion of off-balance-sheet promises slated over the next several years, most of which come due by fiscal 2029. Huang summed up the pivot in August, saying, "We used to build chips that we sell," and, "now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset." On a podcast last week he added, "We're the most rentable. We're fungible, and we're durable."

Demand, he says, is not the bottleneck. Huang told CNBC this week that interest in neoclouds is "off the charts," and said in Berlin that what is missing is "the working capital to fuel that growth," because "there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital." Nvidia declined to comment otherwise.

Nvidia's cash flow is a key edge. Its equity holdings were marked at $99 billion at the end of the second quarter. Revenue in the latest fiscal year reached $216 billion, roughly eight times higher since ChatGPT launched in late 2022.

Across the first six months of the year, free cash flow reached $70 billion, compared with a bit over $4 billion at AMD, whereas Alphabet swung to negative cash flow in the second quarter to finance its expansion. Competition is rising, though, from Google's TPUs in its cloud and AMD's Helios rack launched in July.

Mega guarantees, long leases and who carries the risk

OpenAI's planned site in Pike County, Ohio - the potential world's largest data center - comes with Nvidia's largest guarantee and a requirement that Nvidia hardware be used for at least 20 years. The company backed up to $105 billion tied to chips, land and power for the proposed 10 gigawatt complex. It also signed up for $20 billion of future data center leases it expects to assign to third parties.

Most of these promises only turn into cash outlays if a project participant defaults. Should OpenAI fail to pay or become insolvent, Nvidia may take over the lease, secure a replacement tenant, or request that SB Energy, the landlord, sell the facility. For the latter two, Nvidia agreed to cover any shortfall below a minimum price up to $105 billion, or it could make a lump sum payment to SB Energy. The commitment terminates if OpenAI provides collateral or attains a sufficiently high credit rating.

When market headlines involve complex financing, stay clear-headed with the free Market Briefs newsletter that explains it quickly

At CoreWeave, where Nvidia holds an equity stake, it has committed to purchase as much as $6.3 billion of compute if CoreWeave is unable to sell it otherwise. Backstops vary, including minimum resale prices or minimum hourly offtake prices for GPUs if a lender has to recover assets. For Sharon AI and additional neocloud partners, Nvidia has employed revenue-sharing structures. The company says these AI cloud partners see strong customer demand and healthy pipelines yet require massive infrastructure to fulfill it.

In August, Nvidia said it expanded its lending bench by partnering with six major asset managers in a $500 billion financing initiative that treats compute infrastructure as an asset class, and it includes as much as $125 billion of residual-value guarantees for GPU transactions. It put $2 billion to work in Brookfield's inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund targeting $10 billion, and also agreed to be an LP in KKR's $11 billion Helix Digital Infrastructure vehicle, as well as Valor Equity Partners' $5.4 billion compute-focused fund.

Stress shows up at neocloud partners

Credit is tightening for several Nvidia-linked names. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are each down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave's credit default swap spread moved past 11% as investors paid more for default insurance. The company carries roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, of which approximately $35 billion consists of notes, bonds, and loans, and the yields on its 2031 and 2032 bonds climbed above 15%.

Nvidia has exposure to other neoclouds facing setbacks. The firm holds an equity stake in Australia-based AI cloud company Firmus, which pulled its IPO plans this month. Nscale in the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy each submitted U.S. IPO filings in September, but there have been no updates for weeks.

The stock has not escaped the volatility. Nvidia just posted a third straight down week, and shares are off 7.6% for October, on track for the weakest month since last November. Trainer at New Constructs cautioned, "If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem." Separately, Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management told CNBC last month, "They'll do $700 billion in revenue next year," adding that such scale "affords them the ability to finance some of their customers." During the last six to 12 months, Nvidia's credit guarantees have, for the most part, started kicking in.

What this could mean for your portfolio

Backstops lower borrowing costs and speed rollouts, but they also put more risk on Nvidia if counterparties falter. Investors are weighing how the company might use its cash and its $5 trillion market capitalization to accelerate chip deliveries to customers, along with the risks that approach brings.

In plain English: Nvidia is betting that underwriting today's buildout sells more of its GPUs tomorrow. That edge is reinforced by a full stack of software, services, integrated hardware and financing. The flip side is visible in this month's drops at CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, higher debt costs, and in the question Trainer raised about demand living up to lofty expectations. Nvidia still dominates AI compute, with systems like Vera Rubin - a seven foot rack with 72 GPUs that can weigh about as much as a pickup truck and costs more than $7 million per Morgan Stanley - even as rivals push alternatives.

name: OpenAI
title: OpenAI is locking its most advanced AI models offline after a string of security scares
description:
OpenAI said Friday that its most advanced models will now train without live internet access.
Why is OpenAI pulling the plug on the live web?
OpenAI restarted training on October 1, 2026, under the new rules, and the restrictions will remain until its safeguards justify broader access.
Anthropic took a similar step two weeks earlier by cutting its internal evaluations off from the live internet.
Whether offline training performs as well as training with the open web remains unproven.
text:
Part of me is relieved that an AI lab is hitting the brakes. The other part wishes it hadn’t taken real incidents to get there.

OpenAI said Friday that its most advanced models will now train without live internet access. Instead, they’ll practice on a cached, simulated copy of the web.

Why is OpenAI pulling the plug on the live web?

The answer is both simple and scary: its models kept finding ways out. On September 20, 2026, an internal research model exploited a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver (the system that turns website names into addresses) and briefly accessed the live internet.

In AI safety terms, this is a critical hazard. Once a model can freely interact with the open web, it can access, alter, or attack external systems in ways that are difficult to monitor or reverse.

As a result, OpenAI paused training for 11 days. But this wasn’t an isolated incident. Reports suggest that models pursuing training goals also hacked into external systems while hunting for answers to specific questions they’d been given, and even traded tips on fringe forums.

OpenAI has already warned over 100 organizations about unauthorized activity by its agents (via TechCrunch). What unsettles me most is the logic behind these incidents. The models were chasing ordinary training tasks, not plotting anything sinister, which is less sci-fi but arguably more concerning.

That’s why “just unplug it” no longer sounds silly to me, even though a former OpenAI researcher has said offline training would mean embedding research teams inside data centers.

What changes now, and what should you do?

OpenAI restarted training on October 1, 2026, under the new rules, and the restrictions will remain until its safeguards justify broader access. Anthropic took a similar step two weeks earlier by cutting its internal evaluations off from the live internet. In other words, this is no longer just one lab’s quirk.

Then there’s the side effect. While stress-testing its defenses with teams of agents, OpenAI uncovered a vulnerability in Brotli, a popular compression library (software that shrinks web data), that could let attackers execute code in programs that use it. Fixed versions are available, so if you use affected software, update it now.

Meanwhile, external evaluators METR and Redwood found new weaknesses in OpenAI’s internal monitoring, including one that could hide hundreds of agent actions. They say they haven’t verified OpenAI’s patches.

Whether offline training performs as well as training with the open web remains unproven.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said that export curbs and trade restrictions imposed by Washington have served as a ‘catalyst’ for China’s rapid progress in semiconductor development. Speaking to CNBC on the sidelines of Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference, Huang stated that American regulatory measures effectively pushed China to speed up its own domestic chip manufacturing and strive for technological self-reliance. US export curbs on China

Current US trade rules prohibit the export of advanced processors to China, including Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence (AI) GPUs. Despite these barriers, reports have claimed, several Chinese entities have managed to access that computing power through third-party data centers based in Southeast Asia. Industry experts consider this access crucial to the growing capabilities of Chinese-developed AI models. “We’ve definitely accelerated China’s initiatives, its nationalization of semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, and all of the industrial support that has been put into that sector, and so there’s no question we’ve accelerated that,” Huang said.

‘American technology well prepared’

Even with intensified competition and China’s accelerated domestic initiatives, the Nvidia chief expressed strong confidence in the standing of US technology companies. Huang stated that American tech firms remain “mighty” and are well-prepared to take on competitive pressure “from anybody.”

Rejecting concerns that memory chips will be supply surplus, Huang implied that the ongoing hardware supercycle is not nearing any abrupt end. "One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it," Huang said, underscoring that High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), which is a specialised form of RAM critical for Al acceleration, will continue to see widespread use for years to come. “We're the first company in the world to put LPDDR memory - what goes into your cell phones - into the world's data centers, and it's enabled us to deliver performance that's twice as energy efficient as anything in the world today, and so we're going to continue to use abundant amounts of them as well,” he said.

On Tuesday, he pointed to the recent slowdown in token spending growth, saying the demand curve for compute is flat and highly sensitive to price changes.

So far, the AI payoff for firms has been slow to materialize, implying a growing reluctance to pay for AI services.”

The main determinant in data-center construction models isn’t physical capacity or power, he argued. Instead, it’s the actual price users are willing to pay for compute.

But companies will only pay a high price if it translates to higher revenue growth, bigger profits, or substantial savings—and there its little sign any of those exist at scale, Slok wrote.

“Maybe that will come in the future. Maybe not,” he warned.

On Thursday, he sounded the alarm on “circularity” in token spending. AI companies have already come under scrutiny for financing deals where they provide money or guarantee debt for other companies that are also top customers, raising doubts about how sustainable their growth is.

Slok suggested a similar dynamic exists between AI startups and the venture capital firms that invest in them, saying 80% of the top 1% of AI spenders are VC-backed. In his view, that means startups are paying for their compute bills with venture capital rather than organic earnings.

And on Saturday, he declared AI has “delivered zero financial payoff” to U.S. companies outside of the big hyperscalers. While profit margins and revenue per workers are rising for the so-called Magnificent Seven, the rest of the S&P 500 has seen no such improvement.

Echoing the week’s earlier notes, Slok said Corporate America overall doesn’t need the latest AI model—and doesn’t want to pay for it. But even as AI becomes cheaper and commoditized, mainstream companies may have a hard time using the technology to boost financial results.

“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote. “Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”

His series of notes came as AI-related stocks tumbled, especially chip names, with traders doubting how much longer the capital expenditure orgy can go on. A handful of hyperscalers plan to spend an estimated $800 billion this year, with capex next year seen topping $1 trillion.

But AI companies may find that raising all that capital won’t be as easy. Meta has already issued a lot of debt, and announced this week the issuance of a new class of shares, in part to help CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay for a possible wealth tax in California.

With the social media giant planning to spend $135 billion-$145 billion this year, the cost of insuring Meta’s debt against default ​touched a record on Thursday. Five-year credit default swaps widened 7.6 basis points to an all-time high of ​114.79 basis points.

At the same time, smaller AI companies like “neoclouds” have come under pressure. For instance, CoreWeave stock has crashed more than 30% this month, and its five-year credit default swaps have shot up to 1,145 basis points.

The worries don’t end there. S&P’s Global Head for Digital Infrastructure Mark Habib flagged “interconnected financing structures” between hyperscalers and data center projects or smaller AI companies.

“It is ⁠safe to assume that there is more (debt) out there that we are not seeing,” he ​said during a roundtable in London, according to Reuters.

“If it’s not reported, then it’s not part of the disclosure ​by the hyperscalers. Also, if we are not rating the transactions where this liability may accrue, then the fact of the matter is that we might not have the visibility.”

GSK (NYSE:GSK | GSK Price Prediction) reports third-quarter results on October 28. A $2.2 billion Zantac settlement hits the books this quarter and a failed cough program is still fresh, so this report tests whether specialty medicines can carry the load.

Strong First Half Gives Way to a Messier Third Quarter

Last quarter, GSK grew sales 5% to more than £8.4 billion, and core EPS rose 9%. EPS of $1.36 exceeded the $1.27 estimate. Specialty Medicines grew 14% and Vaccines grew 8%, while General Medicines fell 9%.

Q2 also brought setbacks. Results included a camlipixant impairment after the CALM-2 readout, and the £7.1 billion Nuvalent deal pushed net debt to £22 billion. Management now projects 2026 EPS in the lower half of guidance, mainly from about £160 million of added interest.

Shares closed at $50.75, up 6.26% year to date. Meanwhile, the Q3 EPS consensus slipped from $1.4141 90 days ago.

Consensus Calls for Lower EPS on Higher Sales

Last year’s Q3 included a £268 million CureVac patent settlement, which makes the comparison harder.

Metric Consensus Year-Ago Actual YoY Change Q3 2026 EPS $1.3275 $1.46 -9.1% Q3 2026 Revenue $8.81B $8.55B +3.0% FY 2026 EPS $4.7199 $4.60 +2.6% FY 2026 Revenue $33.90B $32.67B +3.8%

Exdensur, Long-Acting HIV and the Zantac Charge Set the Tone

The Zantac settlement resolves 93% of outstanding U.S. state court cases. It creates a large charge this quarter, but it also ends years of legal uncertainty. The focus will be on how management separates the charge from core results.

HIV remains the engine. In Q2, Cabenuva rose 33%, Apretude rose 39%, and long-acting injectables drove 80% of ViiV’s growth. That shift matters because dolutegravir, about 17% of sales, loses U.S. patent protection in 2028.

Exdensur is the launch to track. Its J-code went live on July 1, and more than 50% of insured patients now have coverage. The key metric will be a clear step-up in new patient starts.

Vaccines need a closer look. Arexvy sales fell 18% in Q1 before an Australian tender helped Q2. Trelegy abandonment is also expected to ease in the second half. On the pipeline, bepirovirsen faces an FDA decision date of October 26, and a neladalkib decision is expected by November 27.

A Clean Legal Slate Raises the Bar on Execution

With Zantac largely settled, the focus moves to the growth engine. Management still targets more than £40 billion in 2031 sales and expects operating profit growth to be significantly Q4-weighted. If specialty growth holds and Exdensur gains traction, the camlipixant failure should look like a contained setback. If either one falters, expect the 2028 dolutegravir patent cliff to dominate the discussion again.

text:
Grocery delivery company Instacart is weighing a possible sale after preliminary discussions with Uber and DoorDash. The Information reported Friday, October 23, citing people familiar with the matter. The report sent Instacart shares up about 9% by market close. The company carried a market value of roughly USD 12 billion at Thursday's close.

Talks about a transaction remain uncertain, and neither a sale nor a buyer has been confirmed. Both potential buyers already compete in grocery delivery as well as restaurant orders.

The Information said the parties had held early conversations as Instacart explored its options. The report did not establish that those discussions would produce an agreement. A sale therefore remains a possibility rather than an announced transaction.

The reported talks also came with a potential price range. Based on takeover premiums of 30% to 40% seen in recent public technology deals, the report estimated a valuation of about USD 16 billion to USD 17 billion. That figure represents a possible transaction value, not a confirmed offer from Uber or DoorDash. Neither company has agreed publicly to pay that amount.

Investors responded differently across the three companies on Friday. Instacart gained roughly 9%, while Uber shares fell about 3%. DoorDash declined around 4% by the close. The market reaction followed news of possible talks, not a completed sale. For comparison, the S&P 500 lost about half a percent and the Nasdaq slipped roughly 0.2%.

Uber and DoorDash did not immediately respond to requests for comment. As a result, the public account of the possible sale rested on reporting about early talks, rather than statements confirming negotiations from the companies themselves.

A takeover could bring together Instacart's online grocery marketplace and retailer relationships with a buyer's delivery network and customer base. For either Uber or DoorDash, that combination could support expansion in grocery orders alongside their existing food delivery operations.

The competition already extends beyond traditional restaurant delivery. Both DoorDash and Uber Eats have been expanding their grocery and convenience offerings. Instacart, in turn, reduced the minimum order for free delivery to USD 10 for Instacart+ members last year, as the rival services pushed further into the category.

Amazon is also expanding its quick delivery service, Amazon Now. The service promises groceries and other essentials within 30 minutes or less. That expansion adds another competitor to a market where Instacart already works with retailers through its established marketplace.

Emarketer analyst Zak Stambor pointed to pressure from two directions. Retailers are developing their own digital sales channels, while larger delivery platforms can offer groceries alongside other services. He said a sale could give Instacart greater resources and reach than it has as a standalone business.

Read More: ChatGPT-powered Instacart Launches New In-App AI Search Tool

Combining Instacart with Uber or DoorDash would expand the reach of companies already active in U.S. food and grocery delivery.

That concern has surfaced before. DoorDash held acquisition talks with Instacart in 2021, when a possible transaction carried a valuation between USD 40 billion and USD 50 billion, according to an earlier report by The Information. Worries about approval under the Biden administration ended those discussions.

Stambor said the Trump administration has shown greater willingness to approve acquisitions. Still, he noted that regulators could require a buyer to sell portions of a business. His assessment did not amount to a prediction that any Instacart transaction would receive approval.

The latest discussions also follow other consolidation activity. Uber agreed in July to buy Germany's Delivery Hero in a deal valued at nearly USD 15 billion.

Founder 250

Quantexa, the global data, analytics and AI software company pioneering decision intelligence, has secured a multi-million-pound, three-year contract with the Insolvency Service.

The partnership will provide the government agency’s investigators with a trusted, sovereign data and AI platform to investigate financial wrongdoing, protect taxpayers and support confidence in the UK economy.

It follows a £175m, 10-year partnership awarded to Quantexa by HM Revenue and Customs in May 2026 to modernise its data infrastructure and enable the use of sovereign, governed AI on a national scale.

Founded by Vishal Marria, Quantexa works across a range of sectors, including banking, insurance and government.

Marria, who was included in BusinessCloud’s Founder 250 list, said: “Each year, over £1bn is laundered by organised crime through high street shop fronts, including illegal mini marts, vape shops and barbers.

“’Phoenixing’ is the pernicious crime whereby directors incorporate companies, take on debts, and then walk away, only to set up a similar business again and repeat the crime.

Quantexa to establish new global HQ in London

“And while our memory of the pandemic may be fading, recouping the billions of pounds stolen by bounce-back loan fraudsters, remains a top priority.

“Fighting these blights on the economy is The Insolvency Service. A small but mighty, 142-year-old government agency now wielding best-in-class AI-enabled network analytics to uncover the relationships linking criminal activity.

“Criminals rely on complexity. They exploit fragmented information, obscure relationships and the time it takes investigators to piece together the full picture.

Connecting data

“By connecting that data and putting it into context, investigators will be able to uncover criminal networks more quickly, prioritise the highest-risk targets and apply their expertise where it can have the greatest impact.

“Human investigators will remain firmly in control of every enforcement decision.

“That last point matters. For AI to earn trust in government, agencies must retain control of their data, understand how insights are generated and be able to trace every decision back to the evidence behind it.

“This partnership has sovereignty, explainability and accountability built in from the outset.

“I’m incredibly proud that Quantexa will support The Insolvency Service in its mandate to protect taxpayers, legitimate businesses, employees and creditors, and to bring those who subvert the law to justice.”

Duncan Beach, chief executive of the Insolvency Service, said: “Our recently published strategy makes it very clear that in this rapidly changing world, we need to modernise the work of the Insolvency Service, and a big part of that is moving more quickly, thinking bigger and making better use of intelligence, data and technology.

“So, I’m delighted that we’ve signed this agreement with Quantexa. It means that our skilled investigators will be able to use technology to find the hidden links between cases much more quickly than they could do alone. That means we will be able to combat misconduct much more effectively and bring to justice those who seek to subvert the law.”

text:
Walmart WMT unveiled a bundled Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus membership option this week in a direct challenge to Amazon Prime AMZN and Costco COST. The joint membership costs $120 per year, which is a saving of $100 per year. It's also $19 cheaper than an annual Amazon Prime membership at $139 and $10 cheaper than Costco's $130 Executive membership but $55 more than Costco's $65 Gold Star membership. The biggest savings are for shoppers who now pay for both Prime and a Costco Executive membership, who would save $149 a year by switching to the bundle.

"This is a direct shot at Prime," United National Consumer Suppliers CEO Brett Rose told Retail Dive. He noted that at $120 per year a member gets a warehouse club, delivery, streaming, and gas thrown in. On paper, Walmart wins the value math easily, highlighted Rose.

“The timing tells you everything. Consumers are stretched heading into the holidays, and memberships lock in loyalty and recurring revenue before the spending gets decided,” Rose said. “Loyalty programs are what keep people coming back. However, not more so than lower prices.”

On Wall Street, Oppenheimer analyst Rupesh Parikh and his team believe consumers are the clear winners from the development due to the stronger combination of perks, the ability to have Walmart and Sam’s Club products delivered to your home with no markups, and minimal incremental costs to upgrade. "This new offering further strengthens Walmart's membership value proposition vs. Amazon Prime and COST. To the extent this membership program takes off, WMT should enjoy incremental wallet share gains, especially on the delivery front, but there is a likely initial P&L headwind near term," advised Parikh.

Looking ahead, the timing of the Walmart WMT just ahead of the holidays could put incremental pressure on Amazon AMZN and Costco COST to dial up promotional activity.

Uber’s CEO Named the Gaps Instacart Could Fill

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said “ultimately, we think grocery and retail can be bigger than our core online food delivery business.” He also said the selection, quality, and reliability of that product “are very, very early in its development,” and that Uber is still developing a supply base “that is trained on shopping and not just delivering.” Those are the gaps a grocery specialist could fill.

The lab will use AI to detect and monitor biological threats, with the funding coming alongside up to £200 million in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, according to a government statement. The lab will also work in partnership with Google DeepMind and life sciences company Basecamp Research, while the government announced a separate £65 million for developing countermeasures for pathogens.

"As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future," said Kanishka Narayan, Britain's AI minister. "That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on."

The lab "will be a major new global institution, bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats and ensure Britain leads the world in AI safety and security," Narayan added.

Its creation makes the government's AI strategy increasingly clear: forming institutions outside of existing government departments to research, monitor and harness different aspects of the technology.

The announcement also included £120 million in extra funding for the AI Security Institute, which is the best-funded government agency focused on regularly evaluating cutting-edge AI models, and £23 million more for the AI Economics Institute, which is being set up to analyze the economic impacts of the technology.

'Honest Broker'

The strategy is a key part of the country's attempt to remain relevant in the AI space despite lagging behind the US and China on cutting edge AI models. It's trying to act as an "honest broker" for monitoring and regulating, and taking a distinct role from the European Union, which has strongly regulated the tech.

"AI is changing both the biological risks we face and the nature of biological discovery, and we applaud the UK government's foresight in opening the AI Biosecurity Lab," said Matt Clifford, who leads International Affairs at Anthropic, and was the Prime Minister's AI advisor until last June.

"Bringing together frontier AI, the UK's scientific strength, and government expertise to detect threats earlier and speed up the development of medical treatments will contribute to the safe deployment of AI across industry and society," he added.

The government also announced £130 million to use AI to identify cyber vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure and the economy and improve the country's cyber defenses. That comes after governments and companies around the world rushed to patch two critical flaws in widely used technology on Thursday, which AI helped to find.

There will also be a £120 million boost to the Sovereign AI Fund to broaden its remit to include physical and industrial AI such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing, and expand its procurement program for British start-ups.

title: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit - CNBC
description:

Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN , all cash-burning companies in Nvidia’s portfolio, are down at least 30% this month.

With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia’s deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements.
text:
Sean Gallup | Getty Images

Nvidia’s emergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners.

After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEO Jensen Huang’s strategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands.

That’s meant taking full advantage of Nvidia’s investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates.

As of its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties.

For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won’t have to pay up unless participants in the project default.

“If the demand for compute doesn’t meet these really super lofty expectations, we’re going to have a problem,” said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview.

Nvidia declined to comment for this story.

watch now

Market conditions may soon test Nvidia’s mettle. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN , all cash-burning companies in Nvidia’s portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default.

Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges.

The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month, as well as Nscale out of the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy. Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven’t provided updates on their plans in weeks.

Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year.

Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is “off the charts.”

“What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth,” Huang told CNBC’s Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company’s GTC conference in Berlin. “Because there’s just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there’s a scarcity of capital.”

Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter.

Building the ecosystem

Investors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers’ hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process.

Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022.

Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia’s flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to a Morgan Stanley estimate.

While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes of Google , which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, and Advanced Micro Devices , which launched its first AI rack called Helios in July.

watch now

Cash is Nvidia’s other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet went cash flow negative in the second quarter to fund its buildout.

That’s a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance.

Nvidia’s most recent quarterly financial filing in August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class.

That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield’s inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR’s Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners’ $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund.

“We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use,” Huang told CNBC, in announcing the agreement in August. “But now, Nvidia’s AI factory platform is really an investable asset.”

Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment.

“We’re the most rentable. We’re fungible, and we’re durable,” he said on a podcast with investor Brad Gerstner published last week.

20 years of hardware in Ohio

While Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space.

Nvidia’s biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI’s forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requires use of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years.

The shift from chips to capital carries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble.

If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia’s guarantee ends.

At CoreWeave, Nvidia’s investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can’t find another taker.

Nvidia’s backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia’s deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements.

“We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand,” Nvidia said in its quarterly filing.

Huang said this week that CoreWeave doesn’t need Nvidia’s backstop and that the neocloud’s cost of capital is decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%.

Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business.

CoreWeave and other neoclouds “will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?” Stutland said. “Is it going to break at some point?”

Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products.

“They’ll do $700 billion in revenue next year,” Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. “That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers.”

Nvidia’s credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its last annual filing, published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements.

Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn’t want to be in the position of insurer, “but they’re willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up.”

“They kind of control how things move,” said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. “They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it.”

Not a ‘complete panacea’

Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs.

“Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem,” said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. “But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions.”

According to research from New Constructs, Nvidia’s net present value of off-balance-sheet liabilities in fiscal 2026 totals over $153 billion, an increase of over $100 billion from last year.

Such liabilities have been growing across the entire AI trade, mainly in the form of lease obligations. Ratings agencies like Moody’s have been sounding the alarm. In 2026, guarantees are the fastest-growing type of off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, the agency said.

Moody’s doesn’t count guarantees as debt when rating corporate buyers, but it’s “something we’re constantly monitoring,” said David Gonzales, a vice president at the agency.

“These things are advanced structures that are unique, and so there is no blanket real approach you can take,” he said. Gonzales said it’s likely that chips will retain “values in excess of contractual residual value amounts” in the near future, which would mitigate risk in many of Nvidia’s financing structures.

Still, how much exposure investment grade AI players can handle is “the question we’re evaluating at all times every day,” Gonzales said.

“It’s the center of all of our discussions right now,” he said.

— CNBC’s Seema Mody contributed to this report.

text:
Medtronic has bundled more responsibility onto Michael Marinaro, naming him president while leaving his existing commercial and portfolio duties intact. The appointment, disclosed in a regulatory filing on 15 October, took effect on 14 October — a consolidation of authority rather than a change of role.

Marinaro's expanded title sits alongside a structural shift that is already complete. Medtronic has finished spinning off the MiniMed Group, which now operates as a standalone company, and it has wrapped up the associated exchange offer, taking its own shares in return for MiniMed stock.

A 5.4-fold oversubscribed swap

The scale of investor appetite for that swap is now clear. Medtronic exchanged its remaining 252,813,348 MiniMed shares through an offer that drew 5.4 times the demand needed to cover it. The oversubscription speaks to interest in the exchange itself, not to Medtronic's future operating performance — and the key point for investors is status: the transaction is finished, no longer pending.

Keeping the two developments apart matters. The Marinaro appointment concerns internal leadership at Medtronic; the spin-off changes the corporate structure. Nothing in the personnel move alone says anything extra about the economic consequences of the separation.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Medtronic?

Five pacemakers win CE marking

On the product front, Medtronic said Monday it had secured CE marking for its Vitalis portfolio. The clearance covers five pacemakers — ReSyncra CSP, Restoria CSP, Refina CSP, Effectra and Confirma — all designed to support stimulation of the body's own conduction system. The milestone is regulatory, spanning an entire product family rather than a single device, and should not be confused with clinical outcomes for other Medtronic products: a CE mark and registry data deliver different kinds of information.

Registry findings arrived Thursday, adding real-world experience with the Sphere-9 catheter and the PulseSelect PFA system. The APEX analysis tracked 1,050 patients with atrial fibrillation across 28 sites and recorded a major complication rate of 1.1%.

REAL PULSE, meanwhile, covered 1,160 patients and reported acute procedural success of 100%, with acute major complications at 0.09%. Both sets of figures concern atrial fibrillation. A separate analysis looked at ventricular tachycardia — a different patient group — where 46 patients produced 87% acute procedural success and an estimated 75% freedom from recurrence at six months.

Medtronic at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

What the pieces add up to

Taken together, the picture is one of separate advances that do not substitute for one another: Marinaro's widened remit, a completed MiniMed separation, CE marking for Vitalis and fresh registry data. They offer concrete markers of organizational and operational progress — but on their own they are not proof of higher revenue or profit.

text:
Week of Friday October 23, 2026

1. Anthropic readying AI Compute & mega-AI IPO: Anthropic’s draft S-1 shows $750+ billion AI Compute Plans, Risk Factors, and AI enterprise growth. First-half revenue rose to about $16.3 billion, from $1.1 billion a year earlier, while compute spending rose to nearly $9 billion. By my math, Anthropic now takes in about $1.81 of revenue for every dollar of compute, up from 63 cents last year. The commitments behind that: about $450 billion of mostly noncancelable cloud contracts with Google, AWS, Microsoft and neoclouds, more than $160 billion for Google TPUs through Broadcom, and up to $150 billion more in talks, per Bloomberg. The $80.7 billion first-half net loss is mostly accounting charges on its fundraising instruments, and about a third of the draft is risk factors, some of them likely uninsurable. My take, from AI-RTZ #1246: of the mega-AI IPOs, Anthropic’s story requires the fewest leaps of AI faith, with revenue now outrunning compute. But the draft puts real numbers on the leaps that remain: a compute bill locked in for years while the builds behind it can slip, concentrated customers, and AI risks the insurers won’t touch, as I laid out in AI-RTZ #1243. Mr. Market sets the final price before Thanksgiving. More here and here.

2. OpenAI’s penultimate private raise: OpenAI is finalizing a $30 billion plus private bridge round at a revised $1.25 trillion valuation, down from an earlier $1.4 trillion number ahead of its expected 2027 mega-AI IPO. The round is led by investors from the UAE and Coatue, with commitments due by October 30. Demand from wealthy private clients came in softer than pitched, per the FT, but even the trimmed price is about 50 percent above OpenAI’s last round in March, at about $852 billion. Alongside it, a big UAE compute deal is under negotiation, even as the war with Iran, including Houthi strikes on Riyadh, led Saudi Arabia to postpone its ‘Davos in the Desert’. My take, from ARD #191: OpenAI has been committed and resilient enough to do what it needs to get things done, and this is no exception. Investors are showing some fatigue after hundreds of billions raised this year, from Google’s $80 billion plus to Meta’s new share class. Expect OpenAI to keep adjusting as needed, especially as new data points arrive from Anthropic’s IPO. In September I called OpenAI the Pepsi to Anthropic’s Coke, in ARD #166. A strong number two, raising tens of billions at a trillion and a quarter. More here and here.

3. Nvidia’s Neocloud backup plan: Nvidia is committing over $170 billion to support Neoclouds like CoreWeave and others, about $164.5 billion in lease guarantees and capacity commitments, plus more than $7 billion invested directly in AI cloud providers. The stress is real: CoreWeave’s shares fell about 20% in a week and its bond yields topped 15%, as rising rates raise the cost of money for the most leveraged builders, per The Information in ‘How CoreWeave’s Debt Binge Brought a Moment of Reckoning’. Firmus pulled its IPO, and Nvidia is now in talks to back it with hundreds of millions more. Neoclouds and enterprises were 45% of Nvidia’s data center revenue last quarter, about $40 billion. My take, from AI-RTZ #1248: the Kingmaker became the AI banker, and now looks more like the neoclouds’ central bank. Nvidia can afford to be the backstop, and it hedges the ‘Frenemies’ building their own chips, as I laid out in AI-RTZ #1234. This is still a financing cycle more than a demand cycle. But those of us who lived through the telecom and fiber boom remember vendors financing their customers. Expect consolidation rather than collapse. More here and here.

4. Meta’s Equity Issuance & AI plans: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg restructured Meta’s capital structure to accommodate California’s billionaire tax, and Meta’s growing AI compute ambitions. Starting in January, every Meta shareholder gets a new non-voting Class C share for each share owned, effectively a 2-for-1 split. Zuckerberg can sell 20% of his new shares right away, including to pay California’s proposed one-time 5% wealth tax, which would otherwise cut his voting control from about 61% to about 53%, per the NYT. He commits to staying where Meta is headquartered for eight years. And Meta can sell the new shares to fund AI without diluting anyone’s vote. It needs it: record revenue, but the first negative free cash flow since its IPO, and about $825 billion of future commitments, mostly AI compute and data centers. My take, from ARD #190: Mark is battening down the hatches, both defensively and proactively, shielding his stake and his super-majority control, and with it Meta’s AI ambitions. A bespoke move for Meta’s realities. A year ago I wrote that Meta’s AI financing deals would be a roadmap for peers, in RTZ #891. Next chapter: raise the money, keep the vote. More here and here.

5. Elon merging SpaceX/xAI/AI/SI & Tesla: As long expected, Elon Musk is planning to merge his two public entities SpaceX and Tesla. Both have formed special committees of independent directors to discuss it, with Musk recusing himself, though he called a merger ‘a good idea’ on SpaceX’s first earnings call, per CNBC. Combined, they would be worth about $3.6 trillion. Musk controls about 84% of SpaceX’s votes but about 20% of Tesla’s, and the deal needs a majority of all Tesla shares. The quarter behind it: SpaceX revenue up 161% to $14.6 billion, and its first profit as a public company, with its AI business, now called Super Intelligence, up ninefold to $7.6 billion, per The Information. My take, from ARD #189: surprise, surprise indeed. When Elon merged xAI and X, I said Tesla was the next likely stop, in RTZ #675, and again when xAI went under SpaceX in RTZ #987. A bigger combined company would also draw more of the passive index money, as I laid out in AI-RTZ #1115. Having run Goldman’s internet research in the nineties, the big question for me is how analysts value a conglomerate of rockets, Starlink, AI, cars and robots. When Elon is laser focused, things get executed. But here he has a lot of things demanding his ‘laser focus’, both in tech and beyond. More here and here.

text:
Major U.S. airlines are increasingly prioritizing higher ticket prices and profitability over filling every available seat as soaring jet fuel costs put pressure on earnings and prompt carriers to reconsider capacity growth heading into 2027.

According to Reuters, executives at Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group are emphasizing stronger passenger yields rather than pursuing additional traffic through discounted fares.

The strategy has helped boost revenue despite relatively flat passenger volumes. Combined third-quarter passenger revenue at the five airlines increased nearly $8.8 billion, or 18%, compared with the same period last year, while passenger traffic grew less than 1%.

Meanwhile, jet fuel prices have climbed approximately 90% since February, outpacing airlines' ability to recover those costs through higher fares. U.S. airfares increased nearly 23% year over year during the seven months through September, according to Labor Department data.

The financial pressure is prompting carriers to take a closer look at their flight schedules and expansion plans.

Six major U.S. airlines are currently scheduled to increase domestic capacity by 3% in the fourth quarter and 3.8% in the first quarter of 2027, according to Airlines for America data. However, executives have indicated that some planned growth could be scaled back if fuel prices remain elevated.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby recently cautioned that published industry capacity plans for 2027 may not materialize, while American Airlines is reassessing whether additional flights can generate sufficient revenue to cover operating costs.

The potential slowdown has implications for the broader aviation services industry. Changes in flight frequencies and airline capacity can influence ground handling demand, staffing requirements, equipment utilization and airport service contracts.

For ground service providers, the evolving airline environment could make operational flexibility and cost management increasingly important as carriers balance capacity, passenger demand and profitability.

title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
description:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.
The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet.
OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet.
The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.
“These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with.
text:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.

The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”

“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”

The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”

Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

text:
Boehringer Ingelheim and Microsoft have agreed to partner to advance AI-backed clinical development.

As a patient-centric collaboration, the joint venture will involve assessing the potential of digital patient twins. The goal is to reduce the number of participants required in control groups, boost the creation of clinical evidence and enhance clinical trial design.

Agnes Heftberger, Corporate Vice President and CEO of Microsoft Germany and Austria, noted that “the collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim brings together pharmaceutical and scientific expertise with Microsoft’s capabilities in AI and engineering.”

Specifically, Boehringer and Microsoft plan use modeling, prototyping and evidence generation to evaluate the scientific and technical feasibility of AI in clinical development. Lung health is the first disease area that will be investigated. Additionally, the partnership will explore advanced trial simulation, including whether these approaches could support synthetic or hybrid control arms.

text:
Instacart is exploring a sale after preliminary talks with Uber and DoorDash, five years after DoorDash discussed buying it at a far higher valuation.

Instacart is exploring a sale and has held early talks with both Uber and DoorDash as potential buyers, according to a report from The Information. The company is working with an investment bank to weigh its options, and shares jumped about 9% to $56.44, pushing Instacart's market value to roughly $12 billion. Nothing is final. The discussions are preliminary and may not produce a deal at all.

Here's the number that actually tells the story. A typical takeover premium in tech runs 30% to 40%, which would put a deal in the $16 billion to $17 billion range. Back in 2021, DoorDash was in talks to buy Instacart at $40 billion to $50 billion, when Instacart itself was privately valued at $39 billion. Those talks fell apart partly over antitrust worries under the Biden administration. Instacart's current market value is less than a third of the valuation discussed five years ago, although any takeover would likely include a premium.

Instacart went public in September 2023 at a valuation already cut down from its 2021 peak, and it has since faced competition from Amazon, DoorDash and Uber. Its business is still growing: orders rose 15% and gross transaction value increased 11% in 2025. Instacart has also diversified, launching an embedded shopping app inside ChatGPT in December 2025 and rolling out AI-powered smart shopping carts with the UK grocer Morrisons. Even so, its roughly $12 billion market value remains far below the $39 billion private valuation it commanded in 2021.

The market's reaction to Friday's news was its own tell. Uber closed down nearly 3% and DoorDash fell more than 4%, according to the same reporting. Investors in the potential buyers, in other words, are not thrilled about the prospect of either company writing a check for Instacart, even a comparatively cheap one. That's a reversal from the breathless tone around the 2021 talks, when a DoorDash-Instacart combination was pitched as a grocery-delivery powerhouse in the making.

What changed on antitrust since 2021

The regulatory backdrop looks different now too. The 2021 talks ended partly because dealmakers worried the Biden-era antitrust authorities would block a combination of two major delivery platforms. The current administration has shown more willingness to settle merger cases through negotiated remedies, but a DoorDash-Instacart combination would still merge two of the biggest players in grocery and restaurant delivery logistics in the country and would likely draw significant scrutiny.

Either acquirer has a clear reason to want this. Uber has been expanding in grocery for years and partnered with Instacart in 2024 to add Uber Eats restaurant delivery to Instacart's app. DoorDash already runs its own grocery partnerships, while Instacart provides enterprise and fulfillment technology to chains including Kroger and Costco. Buying Instacart would give either company immediate access to its established retailer network.

What this really signals is broader than one company's cap table. Grocery delivery never became the standalone, venture-scale category its backers promised in 2020 and 2021. It's turning into a feature that the biggest logistics platforms bolt onto what they already run, not a business that supports its own $40 billion public company. Instacart spent five years proving it could survive on its own. Now it's testing whether it's worth more as somebody else's grocery division than as an independent one.
