text:
A drug once synonymous with rave culture could soon be making its way into a very different setting: the therapist’s office.

A leading psychedelics advocate is “very optimistic” the Food and Drug Administration could approve MDMA-assisted therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder as early as January.

But even if the treatment gets the green light, a major roadblock could stand between the psychedelic and the millions of Americans who could benefit from a new path to relief.

MDMA, also called ecstasy and molly, is known for its euphoric effects and reputation as a party drug. It has no FDA-approved medical uses, though researchers have spent years exploring whether it could serve as a mental health treatment — with promising results.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

In a 2021 clinical trial conducted by the nonprofit Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS), people with PTSD who received MDMA alongside psychotherapy were twice as likely to recover as those who received psychotherapy with a placebo.

PTSD, which can develop after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event, can leave sufferers battling flashbacks, nightmares, severe anxiety and intrusive thoughts, according to the Mayo Clinic.

For patients who’ve exhausted traditional options, advocates have argued that MDMA-assisted therapy could offer a new lifeline.

Yet the road to approval has been anything but a smooth ride.

Two years ago, Lykos Therapeutics looked like a frontrunner to bring MDMA into mainstream medicine.

Then, in August 2024, the FDA dashed those hopes, rejecting the company’s application over questions about the reliability of its clinical trial data, potential safety risks and concerns that the studies didn’t adequately demonstrate the therapy’s effectiveness.

The agency called for another Phase 3 trial to help address those apprehensions.

The decision dealt a major blow to psychedelic researchers, patient advocates and veterans’ groups who’d championed the drug. Had it been approved, it would have marked the first new PTSD therapy in more than two decades.

Rick Doblin — MAPS founder and former board member of Lykos, formally known as the MAPS Public Benefit Corporation — said there had been warning signs before the FDA’s decision.

“Leading up to 2024, I saw a variety of ways in which the management of the company was not responding to the culture, not responding to the critics, not doing proactive things that they needed to do,” Doblin told The Post, describing the saga as a “slow-motion train wreck.”

“I still was surprised that the FDA advisory committee said no and the FDA rejected it,” he noted.

Now, new hope is on the horizon.

In August, Resilient Pharmaceuticals, formerly known as Lykos Therapeutics, reportedly resubmitted its application to the FDA. Notably, the filing did not include the additional Phase 3 trial the agency had previously requested.

Instead, the company cited research conducted by other groups, including a small Veterans Affairs study with long-term follow-up, according to Psychedelic Alpha, which first reported the resubmission.

MAPS confirmed the news, though Resilient hasn’t publicly commented on it. Resilient could not be reached by publication time.

This time around, Doblin thinks the odds are looking good.

“The FDA has sort of put all their concerns on the table, and the company has addressed all those concerns, and the FDA has permitted the new drug application to go forward without another Phase 3 study — that was such a big thing,” he explained.

There are other reasons for optimism, too.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has expressed support for the expedited research and approval of psychedelic therapies for clinical use, potentially bolstering their prospects.

In April, President Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to ramp up psychedelic research. The FDA also issued priority review vouchers to three companies developing psychedelic-based mental health treatments.

“A bigger thing, just from a cultural acceptance point of view, is that the Department of Defense is doing studies with active duty soldiers with PTSD with MDMA-assisted therapy,” Doblin noted.

“I think there’s way more excitement now inside the VA,” he continued. “Plus, you have the entry of big pharma buying up all these companies, which we didn’t have in 2024.”

That includes Eli Lilly, which acquired AtaiBeckley in July for $2.8 billion, gaining access to a pipeline that includes programs based on MDMA.

“I think it’s a completely different situation now,” Doblin said.

At last week’s Beyond Psychedelics Conference in Austin, Texas, Doblin took that optimism to the stage, telling an audience at famed biohacker Dave Asprey’s event there’s a “very good chance” Resilient’s application will be approved by the end of the first quarter of 2027.

His prediction drew cheers from the crowd, a mix of psychedelic researchers, industry insiders and everyday enthusiasts.

“I would say that I’m very optimistic,” he told The Post backstage. “But I’m willing to be disappointed — and we’ll keep trying.”

The FDA declined to comment on the status of the application.

“Under the law, the FDA is able to provide information on approved product applications. Information on an application that has not been approved, including an application yet to receive approval, generally is not releasable,” a spokesperson for the agency said in a statement to The Post.

Even if MDMA clears the regulatory hurdles, another obstacle could throw a wrench in its path to patients: a shortage of qualified therapists that Doblin said is “really acute.”

“The amount of people who need this is astronomical,” he noted. “The VA has estimated there’s 13 million people in America with PTSD — so we have nowhere near the number of therapists we need.”

And Doblin isn’t the only one sounding the alarm.

“Let’s just say we’re already behind,” said Dr. Dave Rabin, a trained MDMA psychotherapist and neuroscientist who studies psychedelics as potential mental health treatments.

“We really need to buckle ourselves in and get ready to create the infrastructure needed for continuing medical education programs,” he told The Post. “That’s the biggest challenge we’re going to have to overcome moving forward — other than insurance reimbursement.”

MAPS is among those working to address the shortage, with the nonprofit planning to hold its first US training in December.

“I think that once it’s approved, there’s going to be even more pressure to expand rapidly because the need is so great,” Doblin said. “But we should be very careful to expand only at the rate that we’ve got qualified therapists.”

text:
Walmart is making some popular GLP-1 medications free for eligible employees with Type 2 diabetes next year. But workers seeking the same drugs for weight loss won’t get the same benefit — a distinction that highlights one of the biggest debates facing employers as they consider coverage in light of soaring costs.

The nation’s largest private employer said that beginning in 2027, it will cover Ozempic and Mounjaro without charge for eligible employees with Type 2 diabetes, subject to prior authorization, according to reports. But coverage comes with an important limitation: Walmart will not cover the medications when prescribed solely for weight loss.

That difference reflects a broader challenge for employers. While GLP-1 drugs have become a flash point in benefits discussions, many companies are drawing a line between treating conditions such as Type 2 diabetes and covering the same medications for weight management.

“More and more companies [are saying], ‘I’ll cover it out of medical necessity. I’m not going to cover it if it’s purely for weight loss,’” SHRM President and CEO Johnny C. Taylor, SHRM-SCP, said recently during a panel at the 2026 EBRI–SHRM Health Benefits Symposium. “Others are saying, ‘I’ll give you both, but you’re going to have different deductibles.’ Then others are not covering it at all.”

Related Tool: GLP-1 Calculator

Employers are increasingly willing to cover GLP-1s for diabetes while remaining reluctant to extend that coverage to weight loss. SHRM’s 2026 Employee Benefits Survey found that 47% of responding employers covered GLP-1s for Type 2 diabetes, compared with 15% for weight management.

Other research points to the same tension. In a July survey by the International Foundation of Employee Benefit Plans, 60% of responding employers said they covered GLP-1 medications for diabetes only, up from 55% in 2025. Just 36% covered the drugs for both diabetes and weight loss, a share that was unchanged from the prior year.

Cost Is Driving the Debate

The reluctance to cover GLP-1s for weight loss isn’t simply a question of whether employers believe the medications work. It’s also a question of how to pay for them — and how to manage a benefit that could be used by a large share of the workforce over an extended period. One in 8 adults are currently taking a GLP-1, according to KFF, and the brand-name injectable drugs typically cost between $1,000 and $1,500 a month for consumers. Employers may foot 70% to 100% of that bill.

As costs rise, a larger share of employers are dropping coverage. Recent figures from the Business Group on Health (BGH) find that 14% of employers have already dropped or plan to drop coverage of GLP-1s for weight management by 2027. Overall, fewer employers are covering GLP-1s to treat obesity, with coverage dropping from 72% in 2025 to 60% in 2026, according to BGH’s survey of 127 employers representing 8.7 million covered U.S. individuals. About a quarter (24%) have never offered coverage and are not considering it, and another 3% are considering coverage for 2028-29.

Starbucks said it will no longer cover GLP-1 medications prescribed for weight loss for benefits-eligible employees, a move that demonstrates how significant the GLP-1 cost burden has become.

“At the end of the day, the biggest issue is cost,” said Eileen Pincay, pharmacy practice leader at benefits and HR consultancy Segal. “We wouldn’t be having this conversation about a drug like metformin, even though that has been used off label for weight loss, because historically it has been pretty cheap. GLP-1s are a different story. GLP-1s work, employees want them, and they’re extremely expensive.”

Flexibility Matters

Experts have argued that employers have to be flexible with design. Kevin Hern, senior vice president of Lilly Employer at Indianapolis-based Lilly USA, said during the EBRI–SHRM Health Benefits Symposium that the financial impact of covering GLP-1 medications depends partly on patients’ health at the start of treatment. People with more advanced obesity-related conditions may see medical costs decline relatively quickly, while healthier patients may initially generate additional costs as they seek more preventive care and routine checkups.

Flexible benefit designs and greater transparency in drug pricing could help employers make better-informed decisions. Hern, for example, cited Lilly’s Employer Connect platform, which is designed to give employers more pricing transparency and flexibility in structuring coverage.

title: R-Calf Weekly Address–Walmart's Beef Empire Threatens Rancher Independence
description:
Walmart later took a minority interest, with board representation, in Sustainable Beef, the Nebraska slaughter and processing company.
In 2025, it opened its own beef cutting and packaging facility in Kansas, supplied by Sustainable Beef.
Walmart itself described this expansion as strengthening supply chain “resiliency and control.” Control deserves our attention.
Sustainable Beef remains majority producer-owned.
Walmart’s Sustainable Beef announcement reaches into grain sourcing, grazing management, animal care, and antibiotic reporting.
text:
A corporation does not have to buy your ranch to take away your independence. It only has to gain enough control over who can buy your cattle—and on what terms.

That is the danger behind Walmart’s expanding reach into the cattle and beef industries.

Walmart is building a system that reaches from cattle genetics to the meat case. Its partner Prime Pursuits sets Angus genetics and production requirements. Walmart’s original supply chain included Mc6 Cattle Feeders for feeding and Creekstone Farms for slaughter.

Walmart later took a minority interest, with board representation, in Sustainable Beef, the Nebraska slaughter and processing company.

In 2025, it opened its own beef cutting and packaging facility in Kansas, supplied by Sustainable Beef.

Walmart itself described this expansion as strengthening supply chain “resiliency and control.”

Control deserves our attention.

Sustainable Beef remains majority producer-owned. Its founders want better returns for ranchers, and new slaughter capacity can create valuable competition. Those are real opportunities.

But breaking the packers’ grip requires more independent competition at every step.

The long-term test is whether producers retain competing buyers, bargaining power, and the freedom to walk away.

R-CALF USA has warned for years that vertical integration can advance through contracts as well as ownership. A corporation can influence production and marketing decisions without buying the land or assuming all the producer’s costs.

Consider three dangers.

First, access to the market.

As a powerful retailer channels more purchases through its own network, independent processors and the cattle producers supplying them can lose opportunities to compete for that business.

If that pattern spreads, producers could face a market divided into corporate supply chains, each deciding who qualifies to participate.

An attractive outlet today can become a source of dependence tomorrow. Even a producer-owned packing plant can lose bargaining power if it becomes heavily dependent on one customer.

Second, the price of your cattle.

Our industry needs buyers competing openly for cattle. Negotiated sales help establish prices used throughout the market, including as benchmarks in many formula contracts.

When cattle are committed in advance without negotiating a firm base price, those cattle can leave the price-setting market while still depending on the prices established there.

USDA has warned that thin cash markets raise concerns about unreliable benchmarks and vulnerability to manipulation.

If Walmart’s model and similar arrangements displace independent bidding, that problem can deepen.

The consequences reach back to the cow-calf producer. What a feeder expects to receive for finished cattle influences what that feeder can pay for calves.

You can be outside Walmart’s program and still be affected by a market with fewer competing bids.

Third, control over the ranch itself.

Walmart’s Sustainable Beef announcement reaches into grain sourcing, grazing management, animal care, and antibiotic reporting.

Quality standards can earn premiums. The danger grows when a producer has so few alternatives that a buyer’s preferences become conditions the producer cannot afford to refuse.

Poultry and hogs show how far that dependence can go.

Poultry growers supply buildings, equipment, and labor, often with substantial debt. Integrators supply the birds and feed and pay growers to raise them.

Hog production has followed a similar path. Under production contracts, farmers raise company-owned pigs, while contractors typically supply feed, make many management decisions, and decide when and where the hogs are sold.

The farmer can still own the farm while depending on a company for the animals and the next paycheck.

Cattle producers should recognize that warning before dependence becomes permanent.

Consumers also have a stake. Efficiency can reduce costs, but lasting competition helps ensure those savings reach families buying beef and producers raising cattle.

We need independent processors with access to customers, vigorous negotiated cattle markets, and producers free to choose among buyers.

Federal antitrust agencies and USDA should examine Walmart’s ownership interests, purchasing arrangements, and supplier contracts together. They should scrutinize restrictions that exclude competitors or weaken producers’ ability to negotiate and enforce the laws that protect competition.

America’s ranching families have invested generations in building their businesses.

Their future must include the freedom to set their own course and bargain for the value they produce.

We’re fighting to keep buyers competing for our cattle and keep independent ranchers in control of their future.

text:
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby has a pointed message for airlines trying to become more premium: copying a better seat does not mean you have copied a better airline. His comparison to putting a Four Seasons room inside a Motel 6 is rather provocative, but I think his underlying argument is sound, provided United remembers that the same standard applies to its own flights.

Scott Kirby Uses Four Seasons And Motel 6 To Explain What Makes An Airline Premium

During United’s October 21 earnings call, Citi analyst John Godyn asked Kirby about competitors pursuing ambitious turnarounds by adding premium seats and changing their fares and fees.

Kirby was dismissive. He argued that an airline cannot selectively copy a few features and expect to reproduce the business behind them.

Then came the hotel analogy:

“You can’t just take a Four Seasons room, copy the room, put it in a Motel 6, and expect it to be a Four Seasons. You need everything else that goes with it, to be successful. There are only two airlines in the country that have been doing it.”

His broader argument concerned reliability, technology, service, and employees who are proud of their airline. He also maintained that the physical onboard product is the easiest part for a competitor to match.

Kirby did not identify a particular airline in that response, though it seems clear to me he was talking about American Airlines and/or Southwest Airlines.

A Better Seat Is Important, But So Is Everything Around It

A Four Seasons stay generally involves much more than the bed or bathroom. You are paying for the way the property is maintained, how employees treat you, and how problems are resolved. A beautiful room loses much of its appeal if it is dirty, the air conditioning does not work, and nobody answers the telephone.

The airline equivalent is familiar.

As I recently experienced on American Airlines, a lie-flat seat is considerably less impressive when its footrest is broken, the power outlet does not work, and the entertainment system is inoperable. The seat itself may have been an expensive investment. But maintaining it is part of delivering the product, too.

The same applies to service. A flight attendant who acknowledges you, responds graciously to a request, and makes an effort when something goes wrong can make a substantial difference. That does not require a new aircraft interior.

Nor can an airline overlook reliability. I am much more likely to remember a six-hour rolling delay than the particular fabric used on my seat.

United has improved in ways I appreciate. Its app is excellent, I love Starlink, and the new United Club I visited in Houston is an impressive investment in the ground experience. Those things work together to give me reasons to choose United.

But none excuses an indifferent crew or a broken seat. Kirby’s argument creates an expectation that United must meet on its own as well…and sometimes falls short, particularly when it comes to service onboard.

United Should Welcome Competition, And Avoid Believing Its Own Hype

I am far less persuaded in Kirby’s confidence that competitors cannot win over loyal customers by improving their products.

That may be true of some travelers, but it is a dangerous general assumption. When it come to my travel, I remain a free agent. United gets plenty of my business because it frequently offers the best combination of schedule, price, and product. Nevertheless, another airline can earn that business when it offers something better.

A lie-flat seat on a route where United offers a recliner is a very practical reason to switch. So is a substantially better departure time. And a competitor does not need to match every part of United’s operation to offer the better choice for a particular trip.

I also welcome American investing in better cabins and JetBlue adding a more useful premium product. Those airlines have work to do, but passengers benefit when they give United a reason to keep improving.

Kirby is right that installing a door on a business class seat does not fix an airline. But it would also be a mistake to dismiss the seat simply because other parts of the operation need attention.

The hotel analogy works in both directions. A Four Seasons name on the building does not excuse a disappointing stay, either. Once you charge more and tell customers they are buying something superior, they reasonably expect you to deliver it.

CONCLUSION

Kirby’s Four Seasons and Motel 6 comparison is valid in the sense that a premium experience depends on far more than the seat. I think United has made substantial progress, and I understand his confidence. But the standard he sets for competitors is one United must keep meeting itself.

A better airline earns its reputation through the flights passengers actually take. I appreciate the investments. Now keep the seats working, the operation reliable, and the service worthy of the premium.

title: Nvidia puts a Vera Rubin AI factory in a shipping container and says it can go live in 14 days
description:
Nvidia wants the AI data center to arrive on a truck.
It describes the design as one of several implementation models under the DSX AI Factory Platform, covering compute, networking, storage, power, liquid cooling, cabling and mechanical design.
It gives no deployment figure, no rack count and no container weight, and it states plainly that containerization is not mandatory for every AI factory.
After delivery there is placement, inter-container connection, hookup to external power, cooling and networking, transport-integrity checks and commissioning.
Shifting the risk in data center schedules For industrial and facilities teams the significance is less the hardware than the shift in where risk lives.
text:
Nvidia wants the AI data center to arrive on a truck. At GTC Berlin on October 21 the company introduced DSX POD, a reference design under which partners build complete blocks of its Vera Rubin AI factory inside standardized containers, integrate and test them before shipment, and connect them to prepared site infrastructure on arrival. Coverage of the launch, including Yahoo Finance and StorageNewsletter, carried Nvidia's claim that deployment at a ready site can fall from roughly six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries planned for early 2027.

The technical blog post by Premal Savla, Nvidia's senior director of product management for DGX systems, is more careful than the headline. It describes the design as one of several implementation models under the DSX AI Factory Platform, covering compute, networking, storage, power, liquid cooling, cabling and mechanical design. It gives no deployment figure, no rack count and no container weight, and it states plainly that containerization is not mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional and on-site builds remain options.

What moves into the factory and what stays on site

What moves into the factory is the work that usually eats a construction schedule at the end. Rack-scale systems are installed in the container, rack-to-rack network cabling, power wiring, control wiring and sensors are connected, and the internal cooling loops are assembled, flushed, pressure-tested and validated. Configuration baselines are loaded and functional tests run against a plan that covers rack inventory, firmware, power-on, fabric connectivity, sensor operation and cooling integrity. The unit is documented, secured for transport and checked again when it lands.

What stays on site is still a construction project. The blog post is explicit that the time saving depends on site teams preparing land, foundations, power and external connectivity in parallel while the containers are built. After delivery there is placement, inter-container connection, hookup to external power, cooling and networking, transport-integrity checks and commissioning. Nvidia's phrase is that on-site work is reduced, not eliminated.

Engineering details and partner list

Two engineering details from Nvidia's post will matter to anyone planning a site. Power enters each core container at a standard 800 volts DC, with the design covering protection, distribution, grounding, rack connections, controls and telemetry from that point inward, while partners engineer the upstream generation and conversion for each location. Cooling is liquid only; Vera Rubin racks require it. The container handles plumbing from the racks to its cooling interface, including manifolds, isolation, instrumentation and leak detection, and the site supplies the water and heat rejection the full loop is commissioned against.

The partner list reported from Berlin spans the system builders and the facilities trades: Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Foxconn's Ingrasys and Bull on the compute side, Schneider Electric and Vertiv on power and cooling, per StorageNewsletter and Engineering.com. Technology.org reported seven Vera Rubin racks per container; that count is not in Nvidia's own material. No pricing was disclosed.

Shifting the risk in data center schedules

For industrial and facilities teams the significance is less the hardware than the shift in where risk lives. Data center schedules have been slipping on exactly the items DSX POD moves off site: cabling, loop flushing, commissioning surprises discovered late with the most expensive equipment already in the room. Factory integration converts that into a repeatable product with a test record, the same move modular construction made for hospitals and prefab made for housing. The trade is flexibility. A standardized container fits a standardized site, and the sites that benefit most are the ones designed around it from the first drawing.

What Happened?

Smith & Nephew held merger talks with Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) to combine with J&J’s orthopedics division.

The Financial Times reported that the talks collapsed over who would run the new company

Talks were reportedly at an advanced stage, and both sides had agreed on the main financial terms and the deal structure. A mid-October announcement was in sight.

Then the talks fell apart. J&J wanted Namal Nawana to lead the merged business, who currently runs J&J’s orthopedics unit. He also led Smith & Nephew for 18 months before leaving as CEO in 2019.

Smith & Nephew wanted its current CEO, Deepak Nath, to stay in charge.

Smith & Nephew had approached J&J earlier this year, and its offer valued J&J’s hip and knee unit at up to $22 billion.

That is almost double Smith & Nephew’s own market value. J&J shareholders would have owned 50.1% of the combined company.

Both companies declined to comment.

See analysts’ growth forecasts and price targets for Johnson & Johnson stock (It’s free) >>>

What the Market Is Telling Us About Johnson & Johnson Stock

The report is unlikely to move Johnson And Johnson stock much by itself. A Mergermarket analyst said it would not be surprising if the two sides returned to the table.

J&J already has a backup plan and announced last October that it would split off orthopedics as a standalone company called DePuy Synthes.

On its Q3 call, J&J said it is leaning toward a spin-off and is targeting mid-2027 for the separation. A CFO also said the business is performing well.

J&J’s Q3 sales were $25.4 billion, up 6%. Innovative Medicine sales grew 7.9%, MedTech grew only 2.5%, and management said that fell short of expectations.

J&J raised its 2026 sales guidance and now expects growth of 6.7% to 7.1%.

Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) shares advanced roughly 2% to $462.42, while Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) stock was essentially unchanged at $33.73. The move in Hewlett Packard Enterprise shares followed fresh AI and industrial edge partnerships plus progress on a lunar computing mission.

HPE stock’s strength stood out against broader market softness. The Global X Data Center & Digital Infrastructure ETF (NASDAQ:DTCR) rose about 2% to $25.39, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) slipped 0.34% to $761.35. Recent announcements around AI infrastructure and frontier computing appear to be supporting the advance.

AI Partnerships Drive Fresh Attention

Hewlett Packard Enterprise expanded its HPE AI Factory offerings with NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), focusing on secure agentic AI for enterprise and industrial settings. The company also deepened collaboration with Schneider Electric to deploy industrial AI agents at the edge using HPE Private Cloud AI. These moves aim to bring intelligence closer to operational environments while addressing data security and cost concerns.

The partnerships highlight Hewlett Packard Enterprise’s push into hybrid and edge AI infrastructure. NVIDIA technologies underpin the expanded capabilities, including support for mixed GPU clusters and agentic workloads. Spaceborne Computer Extends Frontier Story

Hewlett Packard Enterprise announced that its Spaceborne Computer-4 will ride Astrolab’s FLIP rover to the Moon’s south pole later this year. The module is designed to run the first high-performance computing benchmarks on the lunar surface along with AI inference, LiDAR processing, and large-language-model tasks. NASA and Deloitte plan to deploy additional workloads on the system.

The mission builds on earlier Spaceborne Computers that operated on the International Space Station. Hewlett Packard Enterprise is positioning the effort as a step toward edge computing for future lunar exploration and an emerging space economy. The announcement adds a distinctive narrative beyond traditional server sales.

Peers Show Mixed Performance

Dell Technologies stock participated in the AI infrastructure optimism with a solid gain. Super Micro Computer shares, however, held flat after recent volatility in the pure-play AI server segment. The divergence suggests investors are differentiating among suppliers based on partnership breadth and diversification.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise benefits from a mix of enterprise IT, edge, and specialized computing exposure. That mix may be helping the stock hold up better than more narrowly focused peers on a day when broader tech sentiment remains cautious. Data-center related ETFs still advanced even as the wider market lagged.

Sustainability Of Growth Remains The Question

AI infrastructure spending continues to support demand across the server group, yet questions persist about margin durability and valuation after strong runs. Hewlett Packard Enterprise has delivered solid recent gains, but sustaining elevated growth rates will depend on execution in both traditional and frontier segments. title: Eli Lilly breaks ground on $5 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Virginia
description:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA —Eli Lilly and Company has started construction of a $5 billion manufacturing facility in Goochland County, west of Richmond, Virginia, marking another step in its programme to expand pharmaceutical production in the United States.
Lilly has also committed $40 million to support the Virginia Center for Advanced Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, a statewide partnership involving industry, government and higher education institutions.
A hands-on training centre in Goochland County is targeted to open in 2028, helping develop the technical workforce required for advanced pharmaceutical production.
Based in Indianapolis, Indiana, Eli Lilly is a pharmaceutical company engaged in the discovery, development, manufacturing and commercialisation of medicines.
Its investment in Virginia is expected to increase regional demand for construction services, engineering expertise, specialised equipment and pharmaceutical manufacturing talent.
text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA —Eli Lilly and Company has started construction of a $5 billion manufacturing facility in Goochland County, west of Richmond, Virginia, marking another step in its programme to expand pharmaceutical production in the United States. The site will integrate active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) manufacturing with finished-medicine production, making it the company's first facility designed to perform both activities within a single integrated operation. Dedicated capacity will support bioconjugates and large-molecule medicines.

The plant will manufacture antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), a class of targeted therapies that combines antibodies with potent drug compounds to deliver treatment more directly to diseased cells. These medicines are primarily used in oncology, with potential applications also being investigated for autoimmune disorders and other conditions. The facility's specialised production capabilities will support the manufacturing requirements of these complex therapies.

The investment forms part of Lilly's broader commitment to spend more than $50 billion expanding medicine production in the US. Since 2020, the company has announced 10 domestic manufacturing sites covering API production, injectable medicines, medical devices and genetic medicines. The Richmond project adds integrated manufacturing capacity to this network, potentially strengthening the connection between pharmaceutical ingredient production and downstream medicine manufacturing.

For the pharmaceutical industry, the facility addresses growing requirements for specialised manufacturing infrastructure as drug developers advance targeted biologic and conjugate-based treatments. Producing APIs and finished medicines at the same location could improve coordination between manufacturing stages and provide greater control over production processes. Additional domestic capacity may also help support supply continuity, although actual output and its contribution to medicine availability will depend on commissioning, production performance and regulatory requirements.

The project is expected to create approximately 650 permanent positions, including roles for engineers, scientists, laboratory technicians and operations personnel. Construction and the subsequent development of the site are expected to generate around 1,800 construction jobs. Lilly has also committed $40 million to support the Virginia Center for Advanced Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, a statewide partnership involving industry, government and higher education institutions. A hands-on training centre in Goochland County is targeted to open in 2028, helping develop the technical workforce required for advanced pharmaceutical production.

The facility will incorporate artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital integration and advanced data analytics into manufacturing operations. These technologies are intended to improve process consistency, operational oversight and production execution. The site is also targeting Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Gold certification, establishing a sustainability objective alongside its manufacturing expansion.

Based in Indianapolis, Indiana, Eli Lilly is a pharmaceutical company engaged in the discovery, development, manufacturing and commercialisation of medicines. Its investment in Virginia is expected to increase regional demand for construction services, engineering expertise, specialised equipment and pharmaceutical manufacturing talent. For suppliers and service providers, the project may create opportunities across facility development, automation, laboratory systems and ongoing plant operations. Its longer-term strategic significance will depend on the facility's commissioning timeline, manufacturing scale and ability to meet demand for advanced medicines.

description:

text:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) backed OpenAI has reportedly lowered its valuation target to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion as some investors push back against the price of its latest funding round.

The AI company is now seeking up to $30 billion in fresh capital at the lower pre-money valuation, according to a report cited by TipRanks. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are expected to lead the round, while Coatue is also expected to participate.

The change represents a $150 billion reduction from OpenAI's previously reported target, though the new figure remains well above the company's roughly $852 billion valuation in March 2026.

The reason appears to be a more cautious funding environment.

TipRanks said investor demand has been weaker than in previous rounds as concerns grow around the enormous cost of building AI infrastructure and whether those investments will ultimately generate sufficient returns. Some investors may also be dealing with funding fatigue after pouring large sums into AI companies over the past several years.

That concern is showing up elsewhere in the market.

Meta Platforms recently came under pressure despite beating revenue estimates after increasing the lower end of its 2026 capital-spending outlook to $135 billion from $130 billion, while keeping the upper end at $145 billion.

OpenAI itself has told investors it expects to spend roughly $600 billion on computing by 2030, highlighting just how capital-intensive its growth plans have become.

The company is also reportedly exploring additional computing capacity through a commercial arrangement with the UAE.

Investor Takeaway

I think the valuation cut matters less because OpenAI is suddenly worth dramatically less and more because it shows AI investors are becoming more price-sensitive.

A $1.25 trillion valuation is still enormous.

But the fact that OpenAI reportedly had to move down from $1.4 trillion suggests investors are no longer willing to fund AI growth at almost any price.

That is particularly important when the company could spend around $600 billion on compute through 2030.

For investors, the key things to watch are how much OpenAI ultimately raises, the final valuation, the terms of the round, compute spending and whether the company can show operating leverage before a potential 2027 IPO.

The AI funding boom is not disappearing.

But the cost of capital is starting to matter a lot more.

title: Is Ecolab Still The Business You Bought? - Yahoo Finance
description:
On the company's July 28, 2026 call, management said Ecolab had bought the liquid cooling company CoolIT Systems.
Partly: Ecolab's Debt Now Exceeds Shareholders' Equity Ecolab's sales are still growing, but its balance sheet no longer looks like the one you bought.
At the end of the quarter ended June 30, 2026, Ecolab reported total debt of $13.9 billion against shareholders' equity of $10.1 billion.
As recently as March 31, 2026, Ecolab owed $9.27 billion against equity of $10.0 billion.
From March 2024 until Ecolab bought CoolIT Systems, you could assume its debt stayed smaller than its shareholders' equity.
text:
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

If you own Ecolab (ECL), you likely bought the stock for its steady profits. On the company's July 28, 2026 call, management said Ecolab had bought the liquid cooling company CoolIT Systems. So is the Ecolab you hold today the same company you bought?

Partly: Ecolab's Debt Now Exceeds Shareholders' Equity

Ecolab's sales are still growing, but its balance sheet no longer looks like the one you bought. At the end of the quarter ended June 30, 2026, Ecolab reported total debt of $13.9 billion against shareholders' equity of $10.1 billion.

That had not happened in more than two years. From March 2024 through March 2026, Ecolab's debt stayed below its equity for nine quarter ends in a row. As recently as March 31, 2026, Ecolab owed $9.27 billion against equity of $10.0 billion. Its debt then rose by about half over the following three months.

Ecolab Borrowed To Buy CoolIT, And Sales Kept Growing

Ecolab borrowed to pay for CoolIT Systems, and management said its earnings outlook for 2026 includes financing costs from that acquisition. The company also ended the June quarter holding $5.14 billion of cash and short-term investments, compared with $1.92 billion a year earlier. Net of that cash, its debt was $8.78 billion. But the CoolIT deal closed on July 2, after the quarter ended, so the June 30 figures do not yet show the purchase.

The underlying business still looks like the one you bought. Revenue in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, was $4.42 billion, up 9.7% from a year earlier. Ecolab retained 18.2% of that revenue as operating profit, compared with 18.3% in the second quarter of 2025. Management said growth in its global high-tech business, which serves microelectronics and data centers, sped up to 29% in that quarter. So Ecolab's business has held up, and its balance sheet is what has changed.

What Ecolab's Borrowing Means For Your Money

Ecolab said on the call that it was increasing its outlook for 2026. Management now expects adjusted earnings per share of $8.05 to $8.25 for 2026. The $8.15 midpoint is below the $8.53 it forecast in April, but the April forecast left out the CoolIT costs that the new range includes. Management said the range reflects noncash amortization and financing costs from the CoolIT acquisition.

Ecolab still earns far more than its interest bill. Over the twelve months ended June 30, 2026, its operating income was 9.4 times its interest expense. Ecolab's debt rose only in the last three of those months, so that figure includes at most one quarter of interest on the new borrowing.

From March 2024 until Ecolab bought CoolIT Systems, you could assume its debt stayed smaller than its shareholders' equity. You can no longer assume that, though its sales growth and operating margin have held up. When the company reports in October 2026, Ecolab's total debt against its shareholders' equity at the September 30 quarter end will be the number to watch.

Not necessarily on Ecolab alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are. name: Barclays
title: Barclays is latest to redirect spending toward AI as it trims its workforce - Yahoo Finance
description:
The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources.
Barclays The U.K. bank and financial services company revealed in a quarterly financial report this week that it is looking to cut 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of its workforce.
The company said that it was seeking "organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI."
Coinbase The cryptocurrency trading platform is cutting approximately 14% of its workforce partly due to AI.
Snap The owner of social media platform Snapchat is eliminating about 16% of its global workforce, or about 1,000 jobs.
text:
The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources. That can mean an end to some jobs once done by humans. Yet in many cases it means repurposing money once spent on workers so that more capital can be devoted to boosting AI capabilities. Just how much money is being spent on AI is a hot topic as fears of a bubble in the sector grow, but the potential impact on workers in some sectors is clear.

Here's a look at some of the companies that have announced layoffs or hiring reductions this year that are tied in some way to massive spending on AI.

Barclays

The U.K. bank and financial services company revealed in a quarterly financial report this week that it is looking to cut 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of its workforce.

The company said that it was seeking "organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI." Approximately 60% of the cuts will be from support functions, including developers.

Financial institutions are among the most active in deploying AI, in many cases at the expense of workers. Norway's DNB and Commerzbank in Germany have also announced job cuts in parallel with a push into AI.

Kroger

Kroger said last week that it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as the national grocery chain ramps up its use of artificial intelligence.

"Technology is reshaping what's possible," CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees. "The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done."

Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant "to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes."

The Cincinnati company is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith's and Fred Meyer.

Meta

The company that runs Facebook and Instagram said it would lay off about 8,000 workers, or about 10% of its workforce, as it continues to ramp up spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure and highly paid AI-expert hires.

The company said in April that it was making the cuts for the sake of efficiency and to allow new investments in parts of its business, as first reported by Bloomberg, which also said the company will leave about 6,000 jobs unfilled.

Meta had already warned investors that its 2026 expenses will grow significantly — to as much as $169 billion — driven by infrastructure costs and employee compensation, particularly for the artificial intelligence experts it's been hiring.

Microsoft

Software giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to thousands of its U.S. employees.

The company planned to make the offers in early May to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly.

Microsoft has spent billions of dollars operating an ever-expanding global network of data centers powering cloud computing services, AI systems and its own suite of productivity tools, including the AI assistant Copilot.

Standard Chartered

The U.K.-based bank is planning to cut more than 15% of its back office employees by 2030.

Standard Chartered said in May that it was "scaling practical uses of automation, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to streamline processes, improve decision‑making and enhance both client service and internal efficiency."

Coinbase

The cryptocurrency trading platform is cutting approximately 14% of its workforce partly due to AI.

In a blog post, CEO Brian Armstrong said that AI was changing the way that Coinbase worked.

"Over the past year, I've watched engineers use AI to ship in days what used to take a team weeks," he wrote. "Non-technical teams are now shipping production code and many of our workflows are being automated. The pace of what's possible with a small, focused team has changed dramatically, and it's accelerating every day."

Armstrong said that the company needed to take action.

"We are adjusting early and deliberately to rebuild Coinbase to be lean, fast, and AI-native," he wrote.

Pinterest

Pinterest announced in January that it planned to lay off under 15% of its workforce as part of a broader restructuring as the image-sharing platform pivots more of its money to artificial intelligence.

In a securities filing, the company said that it was making the cuts to support "transformation initiatives" — which include reallocating resources to AI-focused roles and prioritizing AI-powered products. It said it was also working to reshape its "sales and go-to-market approach."

Snap

The owner of social media platform Snapchat is eliminating about 16% of its global workforce, or about 1,000 jobs.

"The headcount reduction is designed to further streamline our operations and reallocate resources toward our highest-priority initiatives, leveraging increased operational efficiencies to accelerate our path toward net-income profitability," the company said in a regulatory filing.

CEO Evan Spiegel said in a letter to staff in April that another 300 open roles would not be filled.

Block

Financial technology company Block is laying off more than 4,000 of its 10,000 plus employees, reconfiguring to capitalize on its use of artificial intelligence.

"The core thesis is simple. Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company," Jack Dorsey said in a letter to shareholders in Block, the parent company to online payment platforms such as Square and Cash App. "A significantly smaller team, using the tools we're building, can do more and do it better," he said.

Dorsey's comments explicitly naming AI as a key driver behind the decision were also posted on X, or Twitter, a company he co-founded.

The announcement has sent shares of the company sharply higher this year, up 19%, reversing a 12% decline in the previous year.

description:
Mobility provider Bolt has selected NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack as the software foundation for its European robotaxi program.
The technology is initially expected to be deployed in future Lucid vehicles based on NVIDIA Hyperion.
Einride Adopts NVIDIA Technology for Autonomous Trucks Swedish company Einride is also developing the next generation of its Einride Driver autonomous driving system based on the platform.

New AI Models for Autonomous Vehicle Development NVIDIA also introduced several new AI tools for developing and testing autonomous driving systems.
text:
The platform is designed to support different levels of driving automation, including Level 3 for highly automated driving and Level 4 for driverless operation within defined operational areas. In addition to the hardware, manufacturers will be able to use NVIDIA's Alpamayo Stack software platform or their own driving software. European companies planning to develop or demonstrate applications include Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles, and Volvo.

Another key focus is the development of autonomous robotaxi fleets. Mobility provider Bolt has selected NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack as the software foundation for its European robotaxi program.

The technology is initially expected to be deployed in future Lucid vehicles based on NVIDIA Hyperion. Bolt and NVIDIA plan to jointly adapt the software to European road conditions before integrating it into vehicles from other manufacturers.

Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, and Volvo Expand Their Collaboration

Mercedes-Benz also plans to expand its collaboration with NVIDIA on Hyperion and Alpamayo Stack to further develop Level 3 and Level 4 automated and autonomous driving capabilities.

The automaker also announced that MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO, its driver assistance system developed jointly with NVIDIA, is expected to receive approval for urban point-to-point driving assistance in Germany soon.

Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles also showcased its autonomous ID. Buzz AD vehicle platform featuring NVIDIA Hyperion in Berlin. The shared computing and sensor architecture is intended to simplify the integration of different autonomous driving systems and support the development of mobility and transportation services.

Volvo Cars, meanwhile, plans to combine Hyperion, the Halos OS safety system, and Alpamayo Stack with its own vehicle and safety technologies. The goal is to develop future vehicles capable of navigating complex traffic situations autonomously.

Einride Adopts NVIDIA Technology for Autonomous Trucks

Swedish company Einride is also developing the next generation of its Einride Driver autonomous driving system based on the platform. In addition to Hyperion, the system will incorporate NVIDIA Halos, Alpamayo, and AI models from the Cosmos family.

Further applications are also planned for public transportation. Japanese company TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich intend to use NVIDIA Hyperion to develop and validate Level 4 autonomous driving systems for public transportation in Germany.

In addition, suppliers Aptiv, Valeo, and Schaeffler are developing Hyperion-based computing platforms that automakers will be able to integrate into autonomous vehicles and robotaxis.

NVIDIA Halos SAFE Aims to Simplify Safety Validation

Alongside the expansion of its partner network, NVIDIA introduced Halos SAFE, a new framework for evaluating the safety of autonomous vehicles.

The Safety Assurance Framework for Evaluation is designed to bring together different testing methods, including virtual simulations, software-in-the-loop and hardware-in-the-loop testing, real-world driving tests, and in-service fleet monitoring.

Companies working on the development of corresponding evaluation methods include dSPACE, IVEX, and TÜV Rheinland. Other members of the Halos SAFE ecosystem include Mercedes-Benz, Volvo Cars, and JLR.

New AI Models for Autonomous Vehicle Development

NVIDIA also introduced several new AI tools for developing and testing autonomous driving systems.

With Alpamayo 2 Edge, the company unveiled a two-billion-parameter AI model. Based on NVIDIA Cosmos and optimized for the DRIVE AGX Thor in-vehicle computing platform, the model is designed to analyze traffic situations and plan driving maneuvers at a frequency of 10 Hz.

Other new developments include AlpaJudge, an evaluation model designed to assess the quality of AI-generated explanations for driving decisions, and Foundation4D, which enables automated processing of camera data. New variants of Cosmos 3 Nano are also intended to improve the generation of synthetic training data and the simulation of complex traffic scenarios.

With Alpamayo Agentic Factory, NVIDIA also announced an AI-powered development environment designed to further automate data preparation, model training, and simulation. The platform is scheduled for release in early 2027.

Porsche is also working within the Volkswagen Group on a data-driven development platform that combines NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory and Omniverse NuRec with Microsoft Azure. According to the announced targets, the platform could reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycles by up to 85%.

text:
This story was originally published on Supply Chain Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Supply Chain Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

Levi Strauss & Co. won't see benefits from its beleaguered distribution network overhaul until 2027, according to a Q3 earnings call from Oct. 7.

Despite closing its Hebron, Kentucky, distribution center at the end of Q3, Levi's has been slowed by complexity caused by the number of SKUs it manages and a fire at one of its distribution centers, CEO Michelle Gass said in the call.

The fire "was a big disruption in some of our most important weeks," Gass said, though she noted the recovery has gone smoothly. The damage to inventory was insured and the impact on financial results was not significant, the company said in a securities filing. Levi's did not respond to an inquiry about which facility in its network was impacted by the time of publication.

Dive Insight:

Levi's network transition from an owned distribution center approach to a hybrid third-party-run facility model has been tripped up again, but the company is optimistic about where the journey will end.

Following the closure of the Hebron site, Levi's is focused on working through operational complexities at its Groveport, Ohio, facility, where the Kentucky location's work was moved.

"I think 2027 is very reasonable and realistic to start seeing the benefits. And like I said, closing that Hebron facility was an important milestone to say we have the confidence that Groveport will fulfill our needs," Gass said.

Still, this is the second time that Levi's has had to push back its distribution network overhaul completion date. In January, the company said it would wrap up the move by the end of 2026 after it was forced to continue operations at the owned center in Hebron because the transition to Groveport was taking longer than expected.

The challenges of the continued delay have and may continue to cause shipping delays, order cancellations and increased costs, impacting Levi's relationships with wholesale customers, according to the securities filing.

Other companies also working on distribution network changes include La-Z-Boy and AutoZone. Like Levi's, La-Z-Boy is shrinking its footprint by reducing its total number of distribution facilities and the total mileage products travel. On the flip side, AutoZone said this year it was working on expanding its U.S. distribution center network.

Big Y is putting some promotional muscle behind its new foodservice ordering tools, noting at the top of its website that “your favorite meals are now a click away.”

Dive Brief:

Levi Strauss & Co. won’t see benefits from its beleaguered distribution network overhaul until 2027, according to a Q3 earnings call from Oct. 7.

Despite closing its Hebron, Kentucky, distribution center at the end of Q3, Levi’s has been slowed by complexity caused by the number of SKUs it manages and a fire at one of its distribution centers, CEO Michelle Gass said in the call.

The fire “was a big disruption in some of our most important weeks,” Gass said, though she noted the recovery has gone smoothly. The damage to inventory was insured and the impact on financial results was not significant, the company said in a securities filing.Levi’s did not respond to an inquiry about which facility in its network was impacted by the time of publication.

Dive Insight:

Levi’s network transition from an owned distribution center approach to a hybrid third-party-run facility model has been tripped up again, but the company is optimistic about where the journey will end.

Following the closure of the Hebron site, Levi’s is focused on working through operational complexities at its Groveport, Ohio, facility, where the Kentucky location’s work was moved.

“I think 2027 is very reasonable and realistic to start seeing the benefits. And like I said, closing that Hebron facility was an important milestone to say we have the confidence that Groveport will fulfill our needs,” Gass said.

Still, this is the second time that Levi’s has had to push back its distribution network overhaul completion date. In January, the company said it would wrap up the move by the end of 2026 after it was forced to continue operations at the owned center in Hebron because the transition to Groveport was taking longer than expected.

The challenges of the continued delay have and may continue to cause shipping delays, order cancellations and increased costs, impacting Levi’s relationships with wholesale customers, according to the securities filing.

text:
Barclays is shedding roughly 5,000 positions worldwide as part of an operational overhaul connected to the rollout of AI.

The bank has already phased out 1,000 roles and plans to complete another 4,000 departures by the end of the current year.

The combined reductions represent about 5% of its total global headcount.

Roughly 60% of the planned departures will occur within central support functions, directly affecting roles such as developers.

Geographically, a major share of the losses will hit staff in India, where offshore back-office operations for the UK business are situated, the BBC reported.

The downsizing aligns with the conclusion of a three-year cost-reduction programme.

While activity centres heavily on the UK retail bank, the investment banking unit is also within the scope of the cuts.

Barclays has outlined an additional £1.1bn in financial savings expected from its efficiency drives in 2027.

Bank leadership framed the moves as components of a wider modernisation project rather than an exclusive consequence of automation, terming AI the "icing on the cake" of its broader agenda.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan linked the headcount reduction to large-scale infrastructure investments aimed at refining operational structures.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future," Venkatakrishnan said.

"We will employ the AI at scale. But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake. Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays chief financial officer Anna Cross addressed the operational restructuring during a briefing with financial analysts.

"The changes that we're making in the third and fourth quarters of this year are sizable," Cross said.

"They relate both to the simplification of the organisation and to some of the impacts that we're starting to see from AI."

Competitors including HSBC, Standard Chartered, and Danske Bank have likewise disclosed AI-linked headcount reductions during the year.

The staff cuts drew an immediate reaction from labour union Unite, which represents banking sector personnel.

Sharon Graham, the union's general secretary, stated that the financial institution was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".

"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," Graham said.
