text:
By Echo Wang, Krystal Hu and Sabrina Valle

NEW YORK, Oct 19 (Reuters) – OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fundraising that could value the ChatGPT maker at over $1.4 trillion, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The rapid timetable reflects, in part, a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are increasingly tapping in to a similar investor base, the people said, adding that OpenAI wants ​to capitalize on its recent revenue growth after launching new models. SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round ‌of about $30 billion, one of the people said.

The acceleration underscores how closely the two AI developers are competing for capital as both pursue trillion-dollar price tags, amid growing concern about rising interest rates, significant volatility in technology stocks and rising scrutiny of AI valuations.

OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI’s funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said.

Investors familiar with the company say OpenAI also needs capital to fund its substantial infrastructure commitments and bolster its balance sheet if a deterioration in the IPO markets further delays its ‌planned 2027 ​listing.

Though there is high demand for the shares of both companies, investors face the challenge of evaluating and allocating capital to ⁠two complex, competing offerings within days or weeks of ⁠each other. Some investors view OpenAI’s financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic’s IPO, the people said.

OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment. Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

TRYING TO HEAD OFF COMPARISONS

OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached $50 billion in annualized revenue and expecting that figure to rise to $70 billion by year-end, according to one of the people.

OpenAI has ​also cut prices on its cheaper models, which it said has boosted usage, and told investors it can further lower the price of AI models, the person added.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue reached roughly $65 billion by July, Reuters previously reported. Its quarterly revenue jumped to $16.8 billion in the third quarter from $11.6 billion in the second quarter this year, it told investors, but slowing month-to-month revenue growth ⁠has raised concerns among investors about its valuation.

OpenAI is seeking to complete the fundraising before Anthropic’s financial disclosures ⁠give investors a fuller picture of its business and invite comparisons between the two companies, one person said.

The disclosures could prompt investors to ​press OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar for more details about the company’s revenue growth and financial outlook, the person added. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares ​upfront. It has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. Anthropic told Reuters earlier ‌that it follows established accounting practices.

“OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comp (comparison),” said Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis. “It’s really a two-horse race in terms of being public.”

OpenAI was last valued at $852 billion in March this year, after a record-breaking $122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com, which agreed to invest up to $50 billion in the lab.

The Financial Times previously reported some details of OpenAI’s potential fundraising.

IPO PLANS HIT BY ⁠MARKET JITTERS

A number of companies preparing to go public have decided to wait until after Anthropic’s planned IPO, wary of competing for investor demand amid market volatility and a pullback in AI stocks, bankers and investors said. Some late-stage companies are also timing private fundraising rounds to avoid coinciding with Anthropic’s expected debut, the bankers and investors said.

Some existing and prospective Anthropic investors have argued ⁠for a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion for its market debut — instead of ‌the desired $2 trillion — after the AI startup’s third-quarter results fell short of expectations, Reuters reported last week.

The reassessment comes amid a choppy ⁠market since September, with volatility in oil prices, rising bond yields and growing concerns about AI safety weighing on investor appetite for ​technology stocks. Investors ‌are also scrutinizing the cost of AI infrastructure, including the debt needed to finance the data centers powering the boom.

At the ​center of the latest ⁠concerns is cloud provider CoreWeave, whose shares and debt tumbled last week as investors scrutinized the nearly $50 billion in borrowings used to fund its rapid expansion.

The uncertainty has disrupted what had been expected to be a busy autumn for IPOs, with companies reassessing their listing plans amid market volatility and concerns about valuations. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT, Nvidia-backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either pulled or paused their listings.

Nuclear services company Holtec cited a “perfect storm,” driven mainly by uncertainty around data-center demand, when it pulled its US listing last month.

Companies in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, widely viewed as a proxy for AI-related semiconductor demand, have shed $1.6 trillion in less than two weeks, while AI infrastructure companies have come under particular pressure.

(Reporting by Echo Wang and Sabrina Valle in New York and Krystal Hu in San ​Francisco; Editing by Colin Barr and Matthew Lewis)

title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as 'frontier models can't be trusted'
description:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses.
Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.
OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
text:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

text:
Marinaro’s Expanded Responsibilities and Compensation Details at Medtronic

According to the filing, Medtronic plc’s Board of Directors approved Michael Marinaro’s appointment as President on October 15, 2026, effective October 14, 2026. In this expanded role, Marinaro will maintain oversight of the Medical Surgical Portfolio, Americas, and Global Commercial Operations, while also taking on responsibility for the company’s Greater China operations. These operations will continue to be locally managed by Alex Gu, Senior Vice President and President, Greater China. Marinaro will report directly to Geoffrey S. Martha, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer.

The Compensation and Talent Committee approved Marinaro’s $1,000,000 base salary for fiscal year 2027, with a target annual incentive opportunity of 100% under the Medtronic Incentive Plan. Supplemental long-term incentive awards totaling approximately $3.25 million will be granted on November 2, 2026, under the 2021 Medtronic plc Long-Term Incentive Plan. The $1.625 million performance share unit award will vest on April 27, 2029, based on performance from fiscal years 2027 through 2029. The $975,000 stock option award will vest in four equal annual installments starting August 3, 2027, with a ten-year term. The $650,000 restricted stock unit award will fully vest on August 3, 2029.

The filing also noted that as of the August 21, 2026 record date, 1,279,980,861 ordinary shares were outstanding and eligible to vote. At the Annual General Meeting, 1,116,484,432 shares were represented, establishing a quorum. Besides director elections and auditor ratification, shareholders approved renewing the Board’s authority to issue shares (1,100,821,210 votes for), to opt out of pre-emption rights under Irish law (1,036,661,831 votes for), and authorized overseas market purchases of Medtronic ordinary shares by the company or subsidiaries (1,081,959,682 votes for). The non-binding advisory vote on named executive officer compensation passed with 936,336,164 votes in favor.

Summary of Disclosures

Medtronic plc’s October 19, 2026 Form 8-K detailed Michael Marinaro’s appointment as President with updated compensation, full voting results from the October 15, 2026 Annual General Meeting covering six proposals, and the finalized separation of MiniMed Group, Inc.

text:
Subaru's European range is all Toyota-based EVs from 2028

Subaru will sell no combustion car in Europe after the end of 2027, and the three electric models that remain all sit on Toyota platforms. AutoNext reported last week that the boxer engine is leaving Europe model by model, which leaves the Solterra on the bZ4X, the E-Outback on the bZ4X Touring and the Uncharted on the C-HR+. Subaru's biggest electric car, the seven-seat Getaway, is a Toyota co-development as well. The Sano prototype is the first electric hardware in years that is Subaru's own underneath, and its roughly 2029 timing leaves European dealers selling Toyota-engineered cars alone for at least a year after the boxer goes.

Subaru promised 600,000 electric cars a year by 2030

In 2023 Subaru set a target of 600,000 battery-electric sales a year by 2030, half of its planned global volume, backed by 1.5 trillion yen of electrification spending. By November 2025 it had spent about 300 billion yen, put the remaining 1.2 trillion under review and said it was considering postponing the four in-house electric models it had scheduled by 2028. President Atsushi Osaki said it was appropriate to delay full-scale investment in EV mass production. The Sano mule is what survived that review: a platform, a battery and the electronics, without a launch date. Subaru built 878,016 cars worldwide in 2025, 6.4% fewer than a year earlier, which explains why it is spending carefully.

510 hp, under four seconds and a 100 kg lighter EV platform

Subaru's prototype makes 510 hp through all four wheels and reaches 100 km/h in under four seconds, and its motors are smaller and lighter than those in the brand's current EVs. The architecture targets a weight saving of 100 kg over the electric Subarus built today. The crash structure is new as well: supports curve over the front wheels to spread impact forces, and the front motor is designed to rotate in a collision so that it absorbs energy instead of pushing into the cabin or the battery. The body is an improvised development shell, so it says nothing about the shape of an eventual production car.

Panasonic's 4,000 cells and Aisin's motors power Subaru's in-house EV

The battery holds 4,000 cylindrical cells from Panasonic Energy, and Subaru says it weighs 25% less than its previous pack while aiming for an energy density 20% above the industry average. The drive units come from Aisin, a Toyota Group supplier, so the platform is a Subaru design rather than a Subaru parts list. Both partnerships were signed in March 2024, a week apart. Subaru has not given battery capacity, range or charging speed, which are the three figures a European buyer would compare first.

Subaru's own control unit runs on an AMD chip, not Toyota's Arene

Subaru is developing one integrated electronic control unit to run driver assistance, chassis, powertrain and infotainment from a chip co-designed with AMD. It brings over-the-air updates to a Subaru-developed car for the first time and will support AI functions in a future version of EyeSight. Subaru plans to build the unit itself and use it in electric, hybrid and petrol models alike, and has no current plan to adopt Toyota's Arene software, which Toyota expects to run in 10 million new cars a year by 2030. Its new methods also cut vehicle development time by about 40%, Subaru says.

AutoNext Take

Subaru is not leaving Toyota; it is taking back the parts of the car that make it a Subaru. Aisin still supplies the motors and Toyota still owns about a fifth of the company, but the structure, the crash engineering and the electronics that decide how all-wheel drive and EyeSight behave are now Subaru's own work. For a brand whose buyers chose it for traction and safety more than for an engine layout, that is the half of the car worth owning, and the Sano prototype shows Subaru can still engineer it.

The four in-house EVs promised for 2028 have already slipped once. Subaru's next big stage is the full Japan Mobility Show in autumn 2027, where it showed the Performance-E STI concept last time; if no production body for this platform appears there, no European Subaru built on it will arrive before 2030, and the gap after the boxer will stretch beyond two years.

name: Delta Airlines
title: Delta Just Unveiled Its Biggest Overhaul in 30 Years—Here's What It Means for Premium Travel
description: In a world of airlines stripping amenities to haul more and more passengers, Delta’s overhaul recognizes that luxury at altitude is not just about a seat that lays flat
text:
Summer 2026 is shaping up to be among the most expensive tra…

I have taken over 35 flights this year, so I consider myself…











Photo Credit: Delta Airlines.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines.

Woman sleeping with Missoni bedding and amenity kit in Delta One.

Once you’ve flown long-haul at 35,000 feet, you know that commercial air travel is often the furthest from comfort that one can get. Over the last decades, seats have gotten thinner, legroom has shrunk, hot meals have become bags of pretzels. We’ve learned to pack our own snacks and charge up our noise-canceling headphones because expectations are at an all-time low.

So, when a legacy airline announces its most significant cabin overhaul in nearly 30 years, many of us are curious what these luxury promises entail.

Delta Air Lines has officially pulled back the curtain on a multi-billion-dollar reimagining of its front-of-cabin experience, a total reset of the Delta One journey. Built on 20 years of gathered passenger feedback and backed by sweeping fleet investments, the new debut is bringing real comfort back to commercial air.

The redesign aims to restore the craft and hospitality that flights used to be known for, and it is scheduled to drop first on transoceanic routes before expanding across the carrier’s global network through early 2027.

Here is what flyers can expect.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines

When Delta surveyed its highest-tier flyers about why they drop significant money on premium business class, the answer was overwhelmingly simple: getting good sleep. By angling the suites at 30 degrees toward the windows, designers unlocked three additional inches of bed length—creating an 81-inch lie-flat bed (six feet, eight inches) that comfortably accommodates almost any passenger.

Delta integrated a custom memory-foam cushion that wraps completely around the seat, topped with an additional Missoni-branded mattress pad. Touchpoint details abound: seat controls operate with a smooth, Mercedes-style tactile toggle, a dedicated button tilts the seat into a weight-distributing Zero-G position, and there are even built-in hooks specifically for purses and eyeglasses.

Their sleekest and tallest enclosed privacy doors yet, wireless charging, and mammoth 24-inch 4K QLED screens show their technological advances, plus a 50 times expansion in in-flight entertainment content, giving flyers thousands of titles to choose from.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines

Delta’s culinary team wanted to elevate culinary craft, sourcing and consistency at altitude. To solve the notorious difficulty of serving restaurant-quality food in a low-pressure cabin environment, Delta brought in Michelin-starred Chef Simon Hulstone alongside Master Sommelier Andrea Robinson.

Every dish was re-engineered around altitude-proof physics. A mushroom risotto utilizes specially encapsulated Italian rice designed to withstand the humidity and reheat cycles of galley ovens. A 12-hour braised short rib is paired with a rich potato gratin and reduced jus, while a classic chicken breast is balanced with silky potato purée and roasted onions.

On international routes, regionally inspired menus feature Hong Kong-style sea bass from Chef Jereme Leung, authentic Japanese course dining curated by Chef Norio Ueno, and a custom Wagyu beef burger topped with caramelized onions and cornichons on a brioche bun.

To finish, a dessert cart featuring a dairy-free sorbet float with Champagne Taittinger and an ice cream sundae bar.

Drink options have also gotten a major boost. Bourbon collectors will spot Blanton’s Single Barrel on the cart starting this winter—a rare label rarely seen at altitude. The wine program, crafted with Andrea Robinson, who is an expert on how the palate receives wine at 35,000 feet, leans heavily into California icons like Napa Valley Cabernets and Sonoma Pinot Noirs alongside organic French Chablis. For lighter pours, Delta introduced a cocktail and mocktail lineup featuring alcoholic and zero-proof takes on the Hugo Spritz and Paloma.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines

Passenger autonomy was also on the hit list of the new Delta One design team. Delta expanded its pre-select dining window up to 18 hours prior to departure, allowing travelers to lock in specialized choices—including gluten-free fare, lighter dishes, or pre-arrival plates designed specifically for those who want to maximize sleep and skip the full dinner service altogether.

Service itself features custom, heavy-gauge tableware and redesigned place settings that eliminate clutter on the console.

Partnering with Italian fashion house Missoni, Delta is introducing Winter Elsewhere amenity kits packed with Grown Alchemist skincare, a Marvis dental kit, and Missoni eye masks. On ultra-long-haul routes, a second Missoni Mini pillow joins the bedding setup for enhanced neck support, while cushioned Bombas socks return to keep feet warm during transit.

Even ground connections are expanding: Delta’s signature tarmac transfer program—where select passengers are met on the runway and whisked directly to their next gate—is expanding its fleet of Porsche hybrid vehicles from 40 to 70 across 15 major hubs by 2028.

In a world of airlines stripping amenities to haul more and more passengers, Delta’s overhaul recognizes that luxury at altitude is not just about a seat that lays flat; it’s about hot, Michelin-worthy meals with fresh cracked pepper, a wine that sits well in the mouth at altitude, customizable options, and an experience that leaves you feeling pampered and refreshed when you finally reach your destination.

text:
China-based METiS TechBio (HKEX: 7666), an AI-powered drug delivery company, signed up to a research and discovery collaboration deal with US giant Eli Lilly and Company. Under the deal, METiS will apply its AiLNP platform to develop tissue-specific lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery technologies and is eligible for an upfront payment in the low double-digit millions of USD, up to approximately USD 1.1 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestones, and single-digit tiered royalties on annual net sales of resulting products. The collaboration is at the research and discovery stage; no specific targets, indications, or clinical programs are disclosed. ​

AiLNP is METiS's proprietary AI-driven ionizable-lipid discovery and optimization platform, combining generative and predictive AI for rational LNP design to address the challenge of improving LNP targeting and biodistribution for tissue-specific delivery of therapeutic modalities. The company also highlighted its PhatGPT lipid generative model, although it did not specify any targets, indications, or drug candidates covered by the agreement.

The Lilly agreement adds to a series of partnerships signed by METiS in 2026, which listed to the HKEX in May. In June, the company licensed its preclinical trispecific T-cell engager MTS-128 to Boulevard Bio for USD 20 million upfront and up to USD 1.6 billion in milestones. METiS also established collaborations with Deerfield Management, Hengrui Pharma, and Grit Biotechnology, and reported more than RMB 6 billion in aggregate potential transaction value across its OpenCGT drug-delivery partnerships as of May 2026.

As CEO of the largest, most successful drugmaker on the planet, Dave Ricks sure spends a lot of time thinking about risk. Eli Lilly’s weight-loss and diabetes drugs have become wildly successful beyond anyone’s imagination. It plans to submit a next-gen experimental drug, retatrutide, to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027. All drugs have a shelf life because of how pharma patents work. Likely at some point in the 2030s, the exploding market for its weight-loss drugs will collapse as generics flood in. text:
In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI.

Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing.

The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies.

Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA.

The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI.

Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.”

Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry

Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition.

“We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.”

Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience.

“The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”

Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it.

“That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.”

Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included.

“If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.”

Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution.

“This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.”

Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI.

“I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.”

NVIDIA’s Investments in Germany

Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe.

NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs.

Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace.

Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare.

Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care.

Mirelo, a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen.

Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years.

Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation

Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory, advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%.

NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a record-breaking simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date.

text:
Strategic Architecture and Commercial Analysis of the Stryker and CMR Surgical Partnership

The soft-tissue robotic-assisted surgery landscape is undergoing a structural realignment. For more than two decades,Intuitive Surgical maintained near-exclusive hegemony over general, urological, and gynecological robotic procedures through its da Vinci ecosystem. Over recent fiscal cycles, this market structure has been disrupted by fundamental shifts:key foundational patents have expired, hospital systems have faced mounting capital expenditure pressures, and surgical case volumes have systematically decentralized into outpatient facilities. This changing environment has prompted diversified medical technology conglomerates to establish multi-specialty soft-tissue robotic platforms to protect and expand their operating room franchises.

Stryker Corporation formalized its entry into this clinical arena through an agreement announced on October 12, 2026, committing approximately $400 million (£300 million) in preferred equity to Cambridge, UK-based CMR Surgical. The transaction secures Stryker exclusive commercial agency rights to distribute the Versius robotic portfolio within the United States while granting it an exclusive call option to acquire 100% of CMR Surgical’s remaining equity.

This transaction integrates CMR Surgical’s modular robotic hardware, digital architecture, and international registry of over 45,000 completed cases with Stryker’s commercial sales infrastructure, integrated operating room technologies, and distribution channels across ambulatory surgery centers. The alliance directly counters regulatory clearances gained by Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson MedTech, reshaping how soft-tissue robotics will be capitalised, deployed, and clinically adopted across inpatient and outpatient care environments.

Transaction Architecture and Corporate Governance Integration

The financial and operational structure of the agreement reflects a disciplined, risk-mitigated entry strategy. Soft-tissue robotics platforms historically demand billions of dollars in cumulative research, development, and commercialization costs before achieving sustainable procedural scale. Rather than executing an unhedged, multi-billion-dollar outright takeover of a privately held entity that had previously raised more than $1.6 billion from international investment syndicates, Stryker utilised a preferred equity and agency structure.

This framework grants Stryker substantial operational control and commercial upside in the world’s largest medtech market while limiting balance sheet exposure during early clinical adoption.

The commercial division assigns capital-intensive domestic market entry to Stryker’s institutional sales infrastructure, while CMR manages direct commercialisation and clinical training across mature ex-U.S. programs. Crucially, the preferred equity tranche insulates Stryker by creating an extended evaluation window. Stryker can systematically measure real-world reliability, instrument utilisation rates, customer retention, and recurring procedure margins in American healthcare institutions before establishing a final acquisition valuation.

This arrangement coincides with a planned executive transition at Stryker. On October 6, 2026, Stryker announced that Spencer Stiles, the company's president and chief operating officer, would succeed Kevin Lobo as chief executive officer, effective January 1, 2027. Stiles’ leadership pedigree within Stryker spans nearly three decades, including substantial tenures overseeing Endoscopy, MedSurg, and corporate mergers and acquisitions.

With Stiles stepping into the chief executive role and Andy Pierce joining CMR’s board, executive oversight of the Versius rollout is directly seated within the leadership cohort responsible for Stryker's historical dominance in operating room capital equipment and laparoscopic instrumentation.

System Architecture: Modular Engineering and Procedural Ergonomics

The clinical engineering philosophy behind CMR Surgical’s Versius and Versius Plus platforms diverges from the centralized, single-cart architectures characteristic of traditional multi-arm robotic consoles. Engineered to lower physical barriers to robotic adoption, Versius distributes mechanical manipulators across independent bedside units (BSUs) designed to function inside conventional, non-dedicated operating theatres.

Mechanical Architecture and Bedside Portability

Traditional soft-tissue platforms cluster three to four mechanical arms onto a single, heavy patient cart, which demands extensive floor clearance and dedicated ceiling-mounted booms. Versius uncouples these manipulators into independent, mobile bedside units.

Each BSU features a base footprint of 380 mm by 380 mm, stands 1,425 mm high, and weighs approximately 100 kg. Built on high-mobility casters, individual units can be transported through standard hospital hallways, shared dynamically between surgical suites, and positioned around standard operating tables to accommodate patient anatomy and port geometry.

This modularity eliminates the requirement for structural facility renovations and prevents operating suites from becoming exclusively tied to a single capital device.

Surgeon Console Interface and Open-Field Ergonomics

Versius implements an open-format console designed to address the musculoskeletal strain and team isolation associated with closed, tunnel-vision stereo viewers. The surgeon sits or stands naturally before a polarised 26-inch 3D high-definition display, wearing lightweight passive glasses.

This configuration preserves direct, uninhibited line-of-sight communication with bedside assistants, circulating nurses, and anesthesiologists, enhancing perioperative situational awareness and team coordination. The ergonomic hand manipulators translate manual dexterity into seven degrees of articulation at the instrument tip inside the patient, complete with algorithmic tremor suppression and multi-ratio motion scaling.

Generational Upgrades: The Versius Plus Evolution

The platform entering the United States market is the second-generation Versius Plus. Following his appointment as chief executive officer, Massimiliano Colella delayed the commercial deployment of the first-generation Versius in the United States to wait for the complete Versius Plus hardware and software suite.

Versius Plus incorporates several hardware, optical, and software systems:

Integrated Advanced Fluorescence Imaging (vLimeLite): An integrated near-infrared fluorescence imaging system that visualises tissue perfusion and biliary anatomy using indocyanine green (ICG) fluorophores, toggled via thumbstick controls on the main handpiece without interrupting active instrument manipulation.

Dedicated Advanced Energy Instrumentation: The Versius Ultrasonic Dissector, which combines tissue dissection and simultaneous hemostatic coagulation of vessels up to 5 mm in diameter, powered by a reusable acoustic transducer validated for 25 autoclaving cycles.

Integrated Digital Health Ecosystem: Embedded telemetry platforms, including Versius Connect and Versius Team, which capture intraoperative kinematics, log case metrics, automate video uploads, and deliver software updates without requiring full hardware obsolescence.

Regulatory Trajectory and Indications Trajectory

Achieving clinical legitimacy and economic volume in the United States requires navigating the regulatory frameworks administered by the FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health. CMR Surgical executed a stepped, risk-adjusted regulatory path, transitioning from De Novo classification to secondary 510(k) clearances.

Initial De Novo Classification

Because the initial Versius architecture lacked a substantially equivalent predicate device utilizing independent modular bedside carts, CMR petitioned the FDA through the De Novo classification pathway.

In October 2024, the agency issued a De Novo marketing authorization for the first-generation system, classified under FDA Product Code SCV, specifically for adult patients eligible for minimally invasive cholecystectomy. The submission established mechanical integrity, software risk mitigations, human factors safety, and bench-to-bedside comparability in gallbladder procedures.

Versius Plus 510(k) Clearance

With the De Novo classification establishing the regulatory baseline, CMR secured FDA 510(k) premarket clearance for Versius Plus in December 2025. This clearance expanded labeling to include the second-generation console, the vLimeLite real-time fluorescence visualization system, and modernized articulated tools, specifically retaining adult cholecystectomy as the initial domestic clinical indication.

The decision to pair the clearance with gallbladder removal provided an immediate entry point into high-volume general surgery while supporting subsequent indication expansion.

Gynecologic Submission and International Clearances

Because soft-tissue robotic installations cannot achieve financial sustainability on cholecystectomy volume alone, expanding into the broader pelvic cavity is commercially essential.

On April 29, 2026, CMR formally submitted a 510(k) application to the FDA to expand Versius Plus labeling into benign gynecological procedures, including robotic hysterectomy, myomectomy, and pelvic tissue excision. This application relied on extensive prospective multicenter clinical trials and real-world outcomes collected from CMR’s commercial installed base across Europe and Asia, where gynaecological procedures represent a substantial proportion of overall case volume.

Concurrently, European regulators granted Versius a CE mark expansion in January 2026 for paediatric surgical indications, positioning CMR alongside only two other robotics manufacturers possessing European paediatric certification and reinforcing the safety profile of the modular bedside units.

Strategic Synergies Across Stryker's MedSurg Ecosystem and ASC Penetration

Stryker's corporate strategy centers on category leadership supported by comprehensive integration across operating room hardware, digital workflows, and surgical instruments. The acquisition of Mako Surgical in 2013 provided Stryker with the foundational architecture for orthopedic robotics, driving large market shares across total knee, partial knee, and total hip arthroplasties.

However, the historical absence of a dedicated soft-tissue platform left an adjacency gap within Stryker’s broader surgical portfolio, particularly as outpatient surgical centers demanded flexible technologies capable of crossing multiple surgical disciplines.

Stryker commands extensive real estate in hospital surgical wings through its MedSurg and Endoscopy divisions. The company manufactures and services complete operating theater environments, encompassing the 1688 AIM 4K fluorescence visualization towers, Connected OR routing networks, Operon surgical tables, Accend overhead surgical lighting, and the System 9 fleet of powered cutting instruments.

Versius serves as an electromechanical conduit that enhances these existing product lines. Hospital procurement executives are increasingly directing purchasing dollars toward unified enterprise vendors capable of bundling capital installations, single-source maintenance service contracts, and bulk instrument discounting.

By integrating Versius Plus alongside its endoscopy and orthopaedic lines, Stryker can propose comprehensive institutional agreements that combine soft-tissue robotics, advanced visualisation, and integrated operating room infrastructure within a single commercial package.

This commercial synergy is particularly potent within ambulatory surgery centers. Driven by changes in commercial payer pre authorisation policies and Medicare outpatient prospective payment updates, high-volume elective interventions, most notably cholecystectomy, simple hernia repairs, and benign laparoscopic gynecologic procedures, are transitioning steadily from acute care inpatient theaters to ambulatory sites.

However, traditional soft-tissue robotic systems face structural limitations in ASC facilities:

First, their physical footprints and heavy centralized carts require large, dedicated surgical suites that are uncommon in the square-footage constraints of most outpatient operating rooms.

Second, the capital costs of dedicated systems are difficult to amortize when an operating room must remain flexible enough to accommodate general surgery in the morning and sports medicine or orthopedic repairs in the afternoon.

Versius directly addresses these constraints through its modular portability. Individual BSUs can be unlocked, wheeled down central hallways, and staged in different procedure suites as schedules dictate, or stowed entirely to leave an open floor plan for manual procedures.

Stryker holds a distinctive commercial advantage in this environment. Entering 2026, the company had installed more than 200 Mako orthopaedic robotic platforms in outpatient ASC facilities. Stryker’s commercial representatives already have long-standing relationships with ASC medical directors, corporate chains, and administrative committees.

Cross-leveraging this distribution network allows Stryker to position Versius Plus not as an expensive, isolated capital investment, but as a flexible, multi-disciplinary asset that expands procedural capacity without disrupting room utilization or case flow.

Competitive Dynamics: Confronting Intuitive, Medtronic, and Johnson & Johnson

The alliance between Stryker and CMR Surgical alters competitive dynamics in soft-tissue robotics. The timing of the agreement reflects rising competitive urgency. With rivals Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson receiving clearances for their own platforms, industry observers characterised Stryker's entry as a critical strategic imperative.

Intuitive Surgical maintains an extensive competitive moat. Holding over 70% of the worldwide robotic market, Intuitive expanded da Vinci case volume by 18% in 2025, driven by its multi-specialty footprint and the rollout of the da Vinci 5, which features force-sensing haptics and high-performance computing architectures.

Equity analysts, including J.P. Morgan’s Robbie Marcus, noted that even backed by Stryker’s commercial capabilities, Versius will not displace da Vinci systems within tertiary American teaching hospitals in the near term. Decades of surgeon familiarization, broad specialty clearances, and institutionalized training pathways protect Intuitive’s position in complex inpatient surgery.

Instead, the competitive impact of the Stryker-CMR alliance lands directly upon Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson. Medtronic secured FDA clearance for its Hugo RAS system in urologic procedures in December 2025, initiating initial commercial installations in early 2026 while advancing trials in gynecology and general surgery.

Concurrently, Johnson & Johnson MedTech earned an FDA De Novo authorization on July 22, 2026, for its Ottava platform. Ottava utilises an integrated design that houses four robotic arms beneath the operating table, coordinating movement via Twin Motion technology.

Both Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson have directed their commercial strategies toward large hospital networks seeking alternatives to Intuitive's capital costs and contracting practices. Stryker’s market entry introduces a direct, well capitalised challenger to those efforts.

As Marcus observed, Stryker’s commercial presence is likely to create competitive friction for Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson at the margins. With Stryker focusing its distribution efforts on ambulatory surgery centers and secondary hospitals, Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson must compete against a four-party market dynamic while defending their own procedural indications and hospital capital budgets.

Procedural Economics, Capital Models and Hospital Utilisation

The financial evaluation of robotic platforms balances capital costs, annual service commitments, disposable instrument pricing, and room turnover efficiency.

Acquisition Economics and Alternative Financing

Traditional robotic programs impose significant financial demands: up-front capital requirements routinely exceed $1.8 million to $2.5 million per system, supplemented by service contracts averaging $150,000 to $200,000 annually. For mid-sized community facilities and ambulatory surgical networks running narrower margins, capital payback periods can prove unsustainable without high clinical volume.

First, the baseline acquisition price of the Versius platform ranges between $750,000 and $1,200,000, representing a 30% to 50% discount compared to centralised four-arm systems.

Second, the partners have deployed structured operational leasing and per-procedure commercial models. These models allow facilities to acquire hardware with minimal upfront capital, linking expenses to clinical utilisation via per-case disposable instrument fees (starting around $1,200 per procedure).

Direct Procedural Economics and Micro-Costing Analysis

Because each bedside unit must be manually positioned, draped, and registered around the operating table, initial turnover times can exceed those of single-cart systems.

As surgical teams complete their training curves and standardize cart placement, operative setup times decrease. Once procedural times achieve parity, the structural savings in capital amortisation and consumable instrument packs can generate positive operating margins for high-volume outpatient centres.

Strategic Outlook and Market Implications

Stryker’s investment in CMR Surgical marks the beginning of an era of multi-platform competition in soft-tissue robotic surgery. The transaction highlights several broader market dynamics:

The medtech market is shifting toward distribution-led consolidation. The capital requirements of running multi-specialty clinical trials, meeting heightened post-market regulatory standards under MDR and FDA programs, and supporting large direct-sales fleets have outstripped the capacity of independent venture-backed startups. Future market expansion will increasingly rely on strategic joint ventures, preferred distribution alignments, and corporate takeovers where established medtech leaders supply the commercial scale that emerging robotics platforms lack.

Concurrently, the surgical market is bifurcating by site of care. High-complexity oncology, cardiothoracic, and advanced reconstruction cases will remain anchored within tertiary teaching hospitals, served by comprehensive platforms like the da Vinci 5. Conversely, routine general surgery and benign gynecological procedures are moving toward ambulatory surgery centres and regional community facilities.

By coupling Versius’ modularity and lower capital barrier with Stryker’s outpatient distribution network, this partnership is positioned to contest the outpatient surgical segment.

Finally, the competitive landscape is shifting toward enterprise contracting and bundled equipment suites. The addition of Versius gives Stryker a comprehensive portfolio spanning joint arthroplasty (Mako), operating room visualization (1688 AIM 4K), digital connectivity (Connected OR), surgical tables, and soft-tissue robotics. This breadth allows Stryker to engage health systems and ambulatory surgery networks through integrated, multi-year vendor contracts that create durable competitive barriers against single-specialty device developers.

Over the next 12 to 24 months, the primary execution test for Stryker and CMR Surgical will be converting Versius Plus regulatory clearances into sustained domestic procedural volume. Securing FDA clearance for benign gynaecology remains a critical operational priority to expand clinical utilisation.

Demonstrated procedural adoption and favourable economics across early American hospital and ASC cohorts will ultimately provide Stryker with the clinical and financial validation needed to exercise its option to acquire CMR Surgical outright, cementing soft-tissue robotics as an enduring pillar of its MedSurg business.

title: Microsoft's Nscale exit exposes $103B AI contract pipeline risk - TechTarget
authors: Shane Snider, Sean Kerner, Jade-Ruyu Yan
description:
Microsoft terminated its contract for Nscale's planned AI data center in Essex, England, after a power-delivery delay threatened the project's timeline.
For operators, a missed power deadline can leave planned AI capacity unavailable when needed.
Cordovil recommended separating AI infrastructure announcements into three categories: announced, contracted and energized.
Gartner has warned that substantial AI infrastructure investment could face impairment if projected revenue fails to support the capital committed.
Cordovil cautioned against interpreting Loughton as evidence that AI infrastructure demand is weakening.
text:
Microsoft terminated its contract for Nscale's planned AI data center in Essex, England, after a power-delivery delay threatened the project's timeline.

The setback highlights a risk for data center developers and the operators buying AI capacity: Customer contracts and financing commitments cannot generate revenue until facilities have power and can deliver computing capacity.

For developers, delays can leave construction and financing costs running while customer payments remain tied to delivery milestones. For operators, a missed power deadline can leave planned AI capacity unavailable when needed. Neocloud providers face particular exposure because they often depend on a handful of large customers and borrow against specific deployments.

Nscale unveiled the Loughton project in 2025 as a 50-megawatt campus scalable to 90MW, initially equipped with 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs for Microsoft Azure. The company confirmed through a spokesperson that Microsoft terminated the contract. Nscale remains committed to the site and is exploring alternative power sources and other UK expansion sites. The spokesperson said the broader relationship with Microsoft remains strong and the Loughton issue does not affect other contracts.

The Guardian reported that UK Power Networks had told Nscale it could not supply enough electricity for the site until the early to mid-2030s, years after the project's planned opening. The companies have not disclosed the financial consequences of the termination.

The termination puts a spotlight on the scale of Nscale's contracted business and the conditions required to spark revenue. Its September IPO filing reported $103.4 billion in active and contracted total contract value as of Aug. 31, 2026, compared with $2.6 billion in active contract value.

Microsoft agreements provided for payments of up to $43.8 billion through December 2033, subject to delivery and service-availability requirements. Separate agreements with Anthropic provided for up to $44.6 billion, also subject to delivery requirements. Nscale said it had not obtained binding financing commitments for the GPU equipment and infrastructure needed to fulfill the Anthropic agreements as of the prospectus date.

"Capacity that isn't energized generates no revenue, but the costs keep running," said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell'Oro Group.

Power is the missing link

AI infrastructure projects depend on three elements lining up: a creditworthy customer, financing supported by that commitment, and available electricity, Cordovil said. Developers have more control over securing customers and financing than over when utilities can deliver power.

Grid operators sometimes revise connection commitments by six months or a year, and occasionally longer. Permitting that depends on third parties can also delay projects, he said.

"The problem isn't necessarily that AI demand disappears," said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group. "It's that capital can become committed long before the physical and financial assumptions supporting its recovery are proven."

Neoclouds face concentrated exposure

A delayed site can have a greater financial impact on neoclouds than on hyperscalers, Cordovil said. Neoclouds often have concentrated customer bases, higher capital costs and GPUs financed against specific contracts.

"A hyperscaler can absorb one delayed site across a large, diversified fleet and balance sheet. A neocloud typically has more concentrated customers and a higher cost of capital," Cordovil said.

Losing an anchor customer can leave a provider with equipment and financing arranged around a deployment that no longer has a buyer. Nscale's filing describes multiple financing facilities for GPU equipment and data center infrastructure, but does not establish how much financing or equipment spending was associated with Loughton.

"The issue with neoclouds is that the debt and financing is colossal, and the demand they're betting on is not assured," said Owen Rogers, senior research director of cloud computing at Uptime Institute Intelligence.

Nscale has not publicly detailed the project's spending, termination payments or contractual terms. Those details would help establish how much of the project's financial risk falls on the company, its lenders or equipment suppliers.

Contract value isn't operating revenue

Nscale's filing describes long-term commercial arrangements, including take-or-pay contracts. Its Microsoft agreements remain subject to delivery and service-availability requirements, and contract terms generally commence after GPU clusters or infrastructure have been successfully delivered.

Cordovil recommended separating AI infrastructure announcements into three categories: announced, contracted and energized.

Commitments must also last long enough for providers to recover their investment, Rogers said.

Contracted capacity is meaningless until it's energized capacity,” he said. "Backlog only turns into cash if the neocloud can actually build and power the capacity on time.

Delays can erode GPU returns

Power delays can reduce the time developers have to earn returns on expensive accelerators before newer generations change the economics.

"Nvidia is now releasing new generations roughly every year, so today's best GPU won't be top-end for long," Rogers said. Older hardware can retain value for inference and less demanding applications, he added.

Providers can lose money even when their GPUs remain useful. Late deployment, lower utilization or revenue below financing assumptions can undermine returns, Osnato said. If a provider cannot cover its costs, it may have to sell hardware or the business at a discount.

Gartner has warned that substantial AI infrastructure investment could face impairment if projected revenue fails to support the capital committed. A TechTarget story published Oct. 14 examined that forecast and its implications for the market.

Cordovil cautioned against interpreting Loughton as evidence that AI infrastructure demand is weakening. The problem, he said, is that some project schedules assume grid connection dates utilities cannot meet. Behind-the-meter generation can help bridge the gap, but adds cost, permitting and execution risk.

Shane Snider is a senior news writer at TechTarget, covering AI infrastructure, hyperscale data centers, cloud platforms, and the power and energy systems driving modern compute expansion. You can reach Shane at shane.snider@informatechtarget.com or on LinkedIn.

name: OpenAI
title: OpenAI Confronts Deluge of Social Media-Style Safety Lawsuits - Bloomberg Law News
description:
The litigation targeting OpenAI has clear parallels to youth harm lawsuits facing social media companies that have culminated in almost $1 billion in liability awards from juries, attorneys said.
“The adoption of this new technology was really much, much faster,” said attorney Matthew Bergman of the Social Media Victims Law Center, a law firm dedicated to filing social media harm lawsuits and cases against OpenAI.
It’s a shift from social media cases we’ve seen in the past but it’s a natural progression,” said attorney Jennifer Beckage.
That ultimately led to a record-breaking settlement with Meta this summer to resolve social media safety and privacy claims.
“The state AGs were able to hitch their way into a moving train,” Bergman said of the social media cases.
text:
OpenAI Inc. is confronting a new wave of litigation from state attorneys general and plaintiffs’ law firms who are drawing on the lessons of recent, successful social media harm cases to advance consumer lawsuits against the AI lab.

The San Francisco company was sued by over half a dozen state attorneys general last week alleging it failed to implement sufficient safeguards on ChatGPT to protect vulnerable users including children.

The bipartisan enforcement actions follow numerous individual plaintiffs’ lawsuits, including a proposed class action filed last week, and a similar consumer protection lawsuit brought by the Florida attorney general earlier this summer.

The litigation targeting OpenAI has clear parallels to youth harm lawsuits facing social media companies that have culminated in almost $1 billion in liability awards from juries, attorneys said. Both are using similar product liability and consumer protection theories, but the law firms and state regulators are moving faster and more confidently in seeking to hold AI companies liable for harms caused by their chatbots.

“The adoption of this new technology was really much, much faster,” said attorney Matthew Bergman of the Social Media Victims Law Center, a law firm dedicated to filing social media harm lawsuits and cases against OpenAI.

The alleged harms are much more acute and appearing more quickly: Bergman’s cases deal with ChatGPT users who were allegedly coaxed by the chatbot into killing themselves.

The social media lawsuits alleging inadequate safety features for youths were underway by the time ChatGPT was released to the public, offering consumer advocates such as Bergman a template for seeking to hold AI companies accountable.

“I’m certain the attorneys general are going to question the AI companies: Why did you not build in more controls?” said privacy and tech law attorney Gary Kibel of Davis+Gilbert LLP.

OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to Bloomberg Law’s request for comment for this story. In response to the back-to-back lawsuits last week, the company said in a statement to Bloomberg Law it’s already built “industry-leading age-specific protections” into its product and that it stands ready to work with states to reach “pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry.”

New Strategies, Defenses

Personal injury plaintiffs’ firms were the first to sue social media platforms in the late 2010s using a then-novel theory that apps like Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok are akin to defectively designed products.

Internet platforms for decades have relied for their defense on legal protections of Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act. That 1996 law broadly prohibits lawsuits against websites where the harm stems from content posted by website users. The product liability theory took a different tack, arguing that the platforms were akin to defectively designed products.

The product liability lawsuits expanded against the social platforms beginning in 2022, and courts eventually sided with plaintiffs in agreeing that certain claims could pierce Section 230.

AI lawsuits, so far, have been different. Companies such as OpenAI won’t have the same legal shield that allowed internet companies for decades to fend off any kind of legal challenge. The content at issue is being created directly by the chatbot, not any third-party users.

“It makes sense that these are framed as product design, product liability type cases. It’s a shift from social media cases we’ve seen in the past but it’s a natural progression,” said attorney Jennifer Beckage. Her eponymous firm represents companies on data security and privacy issues.

Attorneys general followed the lead of plaintiffs’ attorneys in the social media cases, bringing a consolidated lawsuit against Meta Platforms Inc. in 2023 in federal court in Northern California representing a bipartisan coalition of over 30 states. That ultimately led to a record-breaking settlement with Meta this summer to resolve social media safety and privacy claims.

In the recent attorney general lawsuits against OpenAI, each of the eight states — Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia — brought separate cases in their respective state courts. It’s a move that the regulators said they hoped will give them more control over the pace and outcome of the cases.

“It is a difficult proposition for a state like West Virginia to go at this completely alone,” the state’s attorney general John B. McCuskey said during a press briefing last week. He added, “We all have our own parents; we all have our own children; we all have our own juries, and it makes sense to all of us to do this in our own jurisdiction but do it in a way that gives us more power as a group.”

The speed and progress of advanced AI has forced everyone to move faster.

“The state AGs were able to hitch their way into a moving train,” Bergman said of the social media cases. “That’s not what you have here.”

text:
The all-stock transaction brings healthcare administration, technology and insurance development businesses under ECGI, although regulatory approvals remain necessary before its planned health plan can operate.

Key Investor Takeaways

ECGI Holdings (USOTC:ECGI) has completed its acquisition of 100% of Avanta Group, expanding into healthcare services and AI-enabled care coordination.

The transaction involved 17.16 million Series A Voting Convertible Preferred shares, with 40% subject to transfer restrictions and performance-based vesting.

Avanta Health Plan intends to pursue Medicare Advantage, commercial and individual insurance markets but has not yet secured the necessary regulatory approvals.

ECGI recently eliminated a $2.556 million convertible obligation as part of its efforts to reduce potentially dilutive debt.

The company's healthcare strategy targets a U.S. market that reached $5.3 trillion in annual spending in 2024, although Avanta's future revenue and enrollment remain uncertain.

Why ECGI Stock Is in Focus

ECGI Holdings (USOTC:ECGI) has completed its acquisition of Avanta Group and its subsidiaries, establishing a foundation for a proposed integrated healthcare platform combining insurance, administrative services and artificial intelligence.

Under the agreement, ECGI issued 17,160,000 shares of Series A Voting Convertible Preferred Stock in exchange for all outstanding Avanta shares.

Of the preferred shares issued, 10,296,000, representing 60%, vested at closing. The remaining 6,864,000 shares are subject to transfer restrictions and performance-based vesting conditions.

The acquired platform comprises several businesses intended to operate across different parts of the healthcare delivery system.

Avanta Health Plan is being developed to provide Medicare Advantage, commercial and individual health insurance products. Avanta MSO is intended to support medical-network administration and operational services.

Avanta Tech will focus on data analytics, automation and AI-enabled healthcare applications, including identifying gaps in patient care, supporting claims processing and improving administrative workflows.

The broader structure also includes Avanta Mart, a proposed consumer-health and wellness channel, and Avanta Properties City Parkway, which is intended to support healthcare infrastructure.

According to ECGI, Avanta's founding team includes executives with experience developing Medicare Advantage plans and medical clinics.

However, the planned health insurance business remains in development and cannot begin operating or enrolling members until the required approvals are obtained.

Why This Matters for Investors

The Avanta Group acquisition represents a strategic shift for ECGI Holdings, introducing exposure to healthcare insurance, technology and administrative services through a single corporate platform.

For investors, the potential significance lies in whether ECGI can establish an operating business that connects healthcare financing, patient services and technology-driven administration.

The company is targeting a substantial market. U.S. national healthcare spending reached approximately $5.3 trillion in 2024, including $1.118 trillion attributable to Medicare, according to figures cited in the announcement.

Medicare Advantage payments are estimated to total $574 billion in 2026, providing context for the sector ECGI intends to enter.

However, these figures describe the broader healthcare market rather than revenue opportunities specifically secured by Avanta.

The proposed integration of insurance, administrative services and AI technology could allow ECGI to coordinate functions that are frequently managed separately across healthcare organizations.

Potential applications include identifying patients who require follow-up care, automating administrative processes, analyzing provider networks and supporting more efficient claims management.

These capabilities may help healthcare organizations address operational costs and improve service coordination, but ECGI has not disclosed commercial performance data demonstrating their financial impact.

Regulatory requirements remain a central consideration.

Avanta has submitted a letter of intent to apply for licensing through the California Department of Managed Health Care but has not yet filed a formal application.

The company also intends to submit a notice of intent to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services later in October 2026. A formal CMS application has not yet been submitted.

Until the required licenses and approvals are obtained, the proposed insurance operations cannot generate revenue through member enrollment.

The acquisition's preferred-stock consideration introduces another factor for existing shareholders. The ultimate impact on ECGI's capital structure will depend on the securities' conversion terms and the performance conditions governing the remaining shares.

Separately, ECGI reported eliminating a $2.556 million convertible obligation earlier in October. That development may reduce potential dilution associated with the retired debt, although the company's overall financial position cannot be assessed from this disclosure alone.

What to Watch Next

The immediate regulatory milestone is Avanta's planned submission of a notice of intent to CMS later in October 2026.

Investors will also be watching for the formal California health plan license application, subsequent regulatory decisions and any indication of when Avanta could become eligible to enroll members.

Further disclosures about the operating status of Avanta MSO and Avanta Tech, including customer relationships, revenue generation and technology deployment, would help clarify the platform's commercial development.

The vesting of the remaining 40% of acquisition-related preferred shares and any additional information about the combined company's financial performance will also be relevant.

For ECGI Holdings (USOTC:ECGI), the central question is whether the completed acquisition can progress from a proposed integrated healthcare structure into a licensed, revenue-generating business.

S&P Global Warns of Undisclosed AI-Linked Debt Among Top Hyperscalers

Analysis of AI-Driven Debt Risks in Major Tech Firms

By Marc Jones

Concerns Over Hidden Liabilities

LONDON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - S&P Global estimates the world's biggest tech firms are likely to have more AI-linked liabilities than currently known, although its top analyst for the sector sees no need to change any ratings at present.

Debt issued by AI infrastructure providers and so-called 'neocloud' firms such as Nvidia-backed CoreWeave has sunk to increasingly stressed levels in recent weeks amid concerns about the aggressive scale of their borrowing.

Risks to Hyperscalers' Ratings

Newsletter Stay ahead of the markets The day's essential banking & finance news, free to your inbox.

S&P's Global Head for Digital Infrastructure Mark Habib said the biggest risk to hyperscalers' ratings remained whether expected profits fail to materialise.

But he also highlighted so-called 'interconnected financing structures', where hyperscalers effectively guarantee huge data centre builds, or smaller AI companies.

Lack of Transparency in Debt Reporting

"It is safe to assume that there is more (debt) out there that we are not seeing," Habib said during a roundtable in London.

"If it's not reported, then it's not part of the disclosure by the hyperscalers. Also, if we are not rating the transactions where this liability may accrue, then the fact of the matter is that we might not have the visibility."

Projected Spending and Financial Outlook

S&P expects the top six US hyperscalers — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Oracle, Meta, and SpaceX — to spend more than $7 trillion on data centers and other AI-related capex between 2025 and 2030, and have negative free cash flow until at least next year.

Habib said there wasn't an estimate of how much additional debt the circular financing might add to firms' balance sheets, although he said S&P was trying to take a "holistic" view overall.

Back in July, it downgraded Oracle to BBB-, the lowest rung of 'investment grade', on concerns about its AI spending and what it called "an uncertain path to profitability".

Market Reactions and Ratings Stability

Habib was also asked whether the recent market selloff of bonds linked to the aggressive AI buildout was a sign that investors see them as riskier than ratings indicate.

"For now, we don't have the view that there is a major disconnect that needs to force our ratings to change at this point," he said, saying S&P's scores were designed to take a longer-term view.

Potential Triggers for Ratings Changes

He said what could change that view was if it became clear the amount of money being spent was no longer sustainable.

"And that could come from a variety of drivers," Habib said. "Further increases in the investments (by AI firms), or a view that the revenue rate of competition is getting too intense."

(Reporting by Marc Jones; Editing by Jan Harvey)

text:
The deal is expected to strengthen the company’s rare disease pipeline with a siRNA asset.

Stock.Adobe.com

Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, has entered a definitive agreement to acquire Silence Therapeutics, a London-based, clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on short interfering RNA (siRNA) therapies for areas of high unmet need.

The all-cash transaction values Silence Therapeutics at an enterprise value of $1.1 billion and an equity value of approximately $1.3 billion, with shareholders set to receive $20 per American depositary share, or $6.6667 per ordinary share, representing an 82% premium to the company’s 30-day volume-weighted average price as of October 16, 2026, the last trading day before the announcement.1

Back in 2017, Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with then CEO of Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany’s healthcare business, Belén Garijo, who touched on the company’s product pipeline. “Our healthcare business is less dependent on Germany and Europe while the product portfolio has broadened beyond our traditional MS franchise to include products in the most promising therapeutic segments, including next generation immuno-oncologic drugs and combinations and in immunology,” said Garijo.

What does the deal include?

The acquisition grants Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, access to Silence’s divesiran, a potentially best-in-class, phase III-ready siRNA investigational therapy in development for phlebotomy-dependent polycythemia vera.1,2

The transaction was unanimously approved by both companies’ boards and is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and a vote by Silence Therapeutics shareholders under a U.K. scheme of arrangement.1 Securityholders representing roughly 14% of Silence Therapeutics’ voting power have already agreed to vote in favor.1 Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, plans to fund the acquisition through proceeds from new debt.

How does divesiran work?

Divesiran is designed to selectively silence TMPRSS6, a gene that regulates hepcidin, the body’s primary iron-metabolism hormone.2 By raising hepcidin levels, the therapy aims to limit iron available for red blood cell production, helping control hematocrit levels and potentially reducing patients’ need for frequent therapeutic phlebotomies.2

In the phase II sanreco study, divesiran met its primary endpoint with an 88% responder rate versus 19% for placebo (p<0.0001), and cut mean phlebotomies to 0.2 per patient versus 2.1 on placebo over weeks zero through 36 (p<0.0001), regardless of background cytoreductive therapy.1 The company reports that the therapy is well tolerated, with infrequent, self-limiting injection-site reactions and two cases of grade 1 anemia assessed by an investigator as treatment-related; no new safety findings emerged.1

Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, frames the acquisition as an extension of its specialty-pipeline strategy. “The planned acquisition of Silence Therapeutics will strengthen our capabilities to serve patients with targeted specialty and rare diseases,” says Kai Beckmann, chairman of the Executive Board and group CEO of Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany. “Following the acquisition of SpringWorks Therapeutics last year, we continue to transform our pipeline toward areas of high specialization and unmet medical need, with an ongoing commitment to external innovation.”

Danny Bar-Zohar, member of the Executive Board and CEO Healthcare at Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, points to the clinical and commercial profile behind the deal. “Silence Therapeutics’ primary siRNA pipeline asset, divesiran, is supported by promising phase II efficacy data, a potentially best-in-class, once-every-three-month dosing schedule, and a safety profile that appears manageable, with the added advantage of targeting a well-defined, homogeneous patient population,” he says. “The planned acquisition also provides an entry point into hematology through a biologically validated mechanism of action.”

What’s next?

Assuming the deal closes as expected in early 2027, Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, intends to advance divesiran into phase III development, betting that its scale and commercial infrastructure can accelerate the program toward patients faster than Silence Therapeutics could alone.1
